De opvoeder kiest voor het kind korte verhalen over de profeten en de rechtschapenen. Hij legt ze hem uit op het niveau van zijn begrip.
Ten tweede: het behandelen ervan door de zuivering van de ziel (tazkiyah)
De opvoeder plant liefde voor de profeten en de rechtschapenen in het hart van het kind. Hij toont vreugde in zijn bijzijn wanneer het de verhalen hoort.
Ten derde: het behandelen ervan door opvoeding — de training van de tong
De opvoeder vraagt het kind na het verhaal naar het beste wat erin zit. Hij prent het het antwoord in als het dit niet weet.
Ten vierde: het behandelen ervan door opvoeding — de training van de ledematen
De opvoeder neemt de verhalen tot voorbeeld in het leven (het eren van de gast, de weldadigheid). Hij nodigt het kind uit om de daad van de Profeet ﷺ na te doen.
Sturing door de vertakkingen van de verheerlijking:
Door de leiding van de ziel en het zoeken van kennis: De opvoeder gebruikt de verhalen om de betekenissen van tawhied en het goede te verankeren, en grondvest zo een referentie waarmee zijn ziel wordt geleid naar Allaah.
Door de leiding van de emoties: Door de verhalen plant de opvoeder liefde voor het goede en zijn mensen en haat voor het kwaad, zodat de emotie van het kind opgroeit op het goede.
Door oprechtheid: Door de verhalen went de opvoeder het kind eraan dat zijn oogmerk het welbehagen van Allaah is, en plant zo oprechtheid.
Door liefde, vrees, loyaliteit en distantiëring: De opvoeder vertelt het kind de verhalen van degenen van wie Allaah hield onder de profeten en de rechtschapenen, en waarschuwt het voor de mensen van het kwaad, zodat het opgroeit met liefde en haat omwille van Allaah.
Door geduld: De opvoeder vertelt de verhalen van de geduldigen om het kind geduld dierbaar te maken, en herhaalt ze totdat zij vast wortelen.
Door oprecht advies: De opvoeder vertelt de verhalen van de geduldigen als een rolmodel, en adviseert het kind zo door hun voorbeeld om het geduld dierbaar te maken en zijn mensen tot voorbeeld te nemen.
Door tijdsbeheersing: De opvoeder reserveert vaste tijden voor de goede verhalen, zodat de liefde voor geduld vast wortelt door bestendigheid.
Door het kennen van de vijanden: De opvoeder vertelt het kind verhalen die de listen van de duivel en zijn vijandschap duidelijk maken, en maakt het zo bekend met zijn vijand en versterkt het.
Toenemend zelfbewustzijn: over zichzelf spreken met het voornaamwoord „ik”.
Deze fase wordt benut om de geloofsidentiteit te versterken: „Ik houd van mijn Heer”, „Ik zeg al-hamdu lillaah”, „Ik bid.”
De uitwerking van het horen en het zien op de vorming van de emoties en het hart
• Positief:
Het horen: Koranische verhalen en doelgerichte liederen planten er de begrippen van waarachtigheid, betrouwbaarheid en moed in.
Het zien: Het zien van rolmodellen in het gebed of in het helpen van anderen plant er waarden in.
Het bewijs: Het woord van Allaah, de Verhevene: ﴿En toen Luqmaan tot zijn zoon zei, terwijl hij hem vermaande: „O mijn zoon, ken geen deelgenoten toe aan Allaah”﴾ [Luqmaan 31:13] — en dit is een bewijs voor het belang van opvoeding door vermaning en de directe aanschouwing van waarden.
• Negatief:
Het horen: Het bespotten van anderen of het gebruik van vulgaire woorden wordt in het geheugen opgeslagen en weerspiegeld in het gedrag.
Het zien: Het aanschouwen van geweld of verraad plant vervormde beelden van de betrekkingen.
De ontwikkelingsovergang en de groei van de zelfstandigheid
• De liefde voor zelfstandigheid bereikt hier een gevorderd niveau:
• Het wil zelf bepalen wat het eet, wat het draagt en waar het heen gaat.
• Het weigert sommige bevelen louter om zijn identiteit te bevestigen.
• Toepassing van het vers:
﴿Nee! Voorwaar, de mens overtreedt * Omdat hij zichzelf als onafhankelijk beschouwt﴾ [al-3Alaq 96:6–7]
En dit komt tot uiting in gedrag dat een evenwicht behoeft tussen begeleiding en vrijheid.
De verhouding tussen het hart en het verstand
• Het verstand begint te denken in de begrippen „oorzaak” en „gevolg”.
• Het hart slaat de gevoelens op die verbonden zijn met waarden en situaties (waarachtigheid = liefde, liegen = vrees of bestraffing).
• De onderlinge samenhang: waarden die worden onderwezen en verbonden met positieve gevoelens raken vast verankerd; maar wanneer zij worden verbonden met wereldse vrees, worden zij mogelijk tijdelijk onthouden, maar niet diep verinnerlijkt. Dit is niet het geval wanneer het de vrees voor Allaah, de Verhevene, en Zijn bestraffing betreft, mits deze in evenwicht is met de liefde voor Allaah (verheven en geprezen is Hij) en het verrichten van het gebod omwille van Hem.
De keuze van de namen
In deze fase dient men te werken op grondslag van de verhouding tussen de dienaar en zijn Heer (verheven en geprezen is Hij):
Het kind begint zijn Heer te leren kennen, en leert wie het is die het moet liefhebben;
Het kind begint zijn Heer te leren kennen door het leren van Zijn schone namen (al-asmaa’ al-husnaa) en Zijn verheven eigenschappen, het voelen ervan, en het toepassen van wat daaruit voortvloeit — en dit is het fundament waarop de latere fasen worden gebouwd, in de mate waarin het kind het begrijpt en waarin de ouders, de opvoeders en de leerkrachten in staat zijn het aan hem over te brengen;
Het kind leert de namen waarmee het in zijn dagelijks leven omgaat:
 Dat Allaah ons heeft geschapen en alles heeft geschapen;
De grootsheid van Allaah (verheven en geprezen is Hij) en dat Hij de Beschikker van alle dingen is;
Dat Allaah altijd alles hoort en ziet, en alles weet — en zo leert het kind over zichzelf te waken, strevend naar het welbehagen van Allaah;
Dat Allaah tot alle dingen bij machte is, zodat het hart van het kind zich aan Allaah hecht;
Dat Allaah alleen het recht heeft om aanbeden te worden, en dat alles Hem toebehoort (verheven is Hij).
De namen die het kind in deze leeftijdsfase (2 tot 4 jaar) zou moeten kennen:
De keuze van de schone namen van Allaah voor kinderen in de leeftijdsfase (2–4 jaar) is niet willekeurig; zij is veeleer gebouwd op een begrip van hun ontwikkelings-, emotionele, cognitieve en gedragskenmerken, teneinde tawhied in hun harten te planten op een wijze die pedagogisch realistisch, taalkundig eenvoudig en emotioneel aangrijpend is.
Waarom concentreren wij ons op deze negen namen?
Waarom juist deze gradatie?
Van het eenvoudige en tastbare → naar het abstracte en begripsmatige
Van wat in de omgeving wordt waargenomen → naar het onwaarneembare dat met het hart verbonden is
De gradatie begint met namen waarmee het kind zich verbindt via de zintuigen (al-Samie3, al-Basier, al-Khaaliq).
Vervolgens verruimt zij zich naar namen die verbonden zijn met gevoelens en geweldigheid (al-Kabier, al-3Adhiem, al-Rahmaan).
Vervolgens ontwikkelt zij zich naar hogere cognitieve en geloofsnamen (al-3Aliem, al-Shaafie)
Deze gradatie draagt bij aan een evenwichtige cognitieve + gevoelsmatige + geloofsgroei.
Kenmerken van het praktisch toepassen van de namen voor kinderen (2–4 jaar)
De gekozen namen houden rekening met de aangeboren en gevoelsmatige groei van het kind en planten het geloof geleidelijk, zodat de islamitische waarden een deel worden van zijn kijk op de wereld, en niet louter uit het hoofd geleerde leuzen.
sections.title_nl: De vier trajecten van de rabbaanie-opvoeding (tarbiyah) voor deze leeftijdscategorie
sections.content_en:
These four tracks are the foundational framework by which the innate traits of this age group are directed and steered; for rabbaanie upbringing (tarbiyah) does not deal with the innate traits singly and in scattered fashion, but organizes them into four tracks issuing from the methodology of purging (tasfiyah), purification of the soul (tazkiyah), and upbringing laid down in Part Two: the track of applying tasfiyah (the formation of thought), the track of applying tazkiyah (the formation of the heart), the track of applying the upbringing of the tongue (the formation of speech), and the track of the upbringing of the limbs (the formation of deeds). Each track has a foundational grounding with its rules and their evidences from the Book and the Sunnah, together with the point of evidence and a fitrah-based rationale that links the rule to the governing trait; then three methods for its application through nine means; then three challenges and their remedy in accordance with the innate traits. Then come the innate characteristics of this age group in detail, to be read and directed in the light of these four tracks.
The First Track: The Track of Applying Tasfiyah
First: The Foundational Grounding — Rules for Applying the Track for This Age Group
The First Rule: Tasfiyah at this age combines the initial implanting of the correct conception and the prevention of falsehood’s entry, both together.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿And Allaah has extracted you from the wombs of your mothers not knowing a thing, and He made for you hearing and vision and hearts that perhaps you would be grateful﴾ [al-Nahl 16:78].
The point of evidence: He (glorified is He) informed that the human being begins devoid of knowledge, and that the senses and the heart are the instruments of acquiring it; this indicates that the educator’s task at this age is to fill this emptiness with the correct conception from the outset, not merely to repel error.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Aboe Hurayrah (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “There is no newborn but that it is born upon the fitrah; then its parents make it a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian.”
The point of evidence: It established that the child is born upon a sound original disposition, and that the external influence either preserves it or distorts it; thus the hadieth brings together both matters: nurturing the sound origin and screening off what distorts.
The fitrah-based rationale: These two evidences were chosen for this age group precisely because a number of its innate traits converge: the rapidity of being influenced by the images of the environment makes the child like a tablet prepared for inscription, which accords with ﴿not knowing a thing﴾; the love of imitation makes him copy what he sees without scrutiny, which accords with “then its parents make it a Jew”; and the emptiness of his mind of any entrenched misconception opens the door for implanting. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: rapidity of impressionability and reception.
The Second Rule: The address must be concrete, in the measure of the child’s faculties, so that the unseen is brought near through the witnessed.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿Then do they not look at the camels — how they are created? And at the sky — how it is raised?﴾ [al-Ghaashiyah 88:17-18].
The point of evidence: The Qur’an adduced as proof of the Creator concrete, observable things (the camels, the sky), addressing the senses before the abstract intellect; this indicates the legitimacy of bringing the meanings of Lordship near to the young through what he sees and touches.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Ibn 3Abbaas (may Allaah be pleased with them both): “O young lad, I shall teach you some words: be mindful of Allaah and He will protect you; be mindful of Allaah and you will find Him before you.”
The point of evidence: The Prophet ﷺ addressed the lad with concise words of tangible effect, suited to his faculties, and did not deliver to him an abstract theological exposition; this indicates the obligation of observing the measure of the one addressed.
The fitrah-based rationale: We mediate through the concrete precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of sensory and motor exploration, the predominance of sensory perception over abstraction, and the love of discovery; the child knows his world through his senses, the verse of al-Ghaashiyah turns his gaze to something concrete, and the Prophet’s ﷺ address came in the measure of his perception. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of sensory exploration.
The Third Rule: Consolidation is achieved through repetition joined with love, not through argumentation and disputation.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿And We have certainly diversified [the contents] in this Qur’an that they may be reminded﴾ [al-Israa’ 17:41].
The point of evidence: He informed that He varied the meanings and repeated them in diverse forms for the sake of remembrance; this indicates that repetition is a legitimate means of entrenchment.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Anas (may Allaah be pleased with him): “And when he ﷺ spoke a word, he would repeat it three times until it was understood from him.”
The point of evidence: It was part of his guidance ﷺ to repeat the word so as to consolidate its understanding; this indicates that repetition is among the methods of prophetic instruction.
The fitrah-based rationale: Repetition was adopted precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of routine and rhythm, the weakness of retention in memory, and finding reassurance in what recurs; what is repeated becomes fixed with the child, and the Qur’an’s varied presentation and the Prophet’s ﷺ repetition of the word accord with that. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of routine and rhythm.
The Fourth Rule: The safeguarding of the fitrah is achieved by giving precedence to the negation of falsehood and the screening of its sources (emptying before adorning).
The evidence from the Book: ﴿And [mention] when Luqmaan said to his son while he was instructing him, “O my son, do not associate [anything] with Allaah. Indeed, association [with Him] is great injustice”﴾ [Luqmaan 31:13].
The point of evidence: The wise man opened the exhortation of his son by purifying his conception of the greatest falsehood (shirk) before building up the affirmative; this indicates that tasfiyah is commenced with the negation of falsehood.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Aboe Hurayrah (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “A man follows the religion of his intimate friend; so let each of you look to whom he takes as intimate friend.”
The point of evidence: He informed that a person is influenced by the religion of the one he consorts with; this indicates the obligation to safeguard the young from the influence that corrupts his conception.
The fitrah-based rationale: Screening and purification were given precedence precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of imitation and emulation of the role model, the rapidity of being influenced by what is seen and heard, and the absence of critical discernment; the child copies the behavior of those around him without scrutiny, Luqmaan’s counsel began with the negation of shirk, and the hadieth “a man follows the religion of his intimate friend” establishes the influence of the companion. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of imitation and emulation.
Second: Three Methods for Applying the Track, Each Method with Three Means
The First Method — graduated, concrete faith-instruction (talqien): (a) the good word joined to the concrete situation, such as saying “Allaah has provided for us” at mealtime and “Allaah has sent it down” at rainfall; (b) answering his fitrah-born questions truthfully and simply, and linking them to the Creator; (c) incorporating the repeated vocabulary of faith into his linguistic stock, such as “Bismillaah” and “al-hamdu lillaah”.
The Second Method — sensory depiction of the correct meaning: (a) short stories that embody tawhied through heroes who love Allaah; (b) faith-imbued sights and sounds, such as the adhaan, images of the Ka3bah, and songs of sound meaning; (c) the visible role model in the places of worship, so that he sees the effect of veneration with his own eyes.
The Third Method — preventive preparation of the mental environment: (a) selecting the auditory and visual inputs and screening out whatever corrupts; (b) correcting the erroneous utterance the moment it occurs, gently and with a sound alternative; (c) regulating the role models of the surroundings and diffusing the majestic name of Allaah with love, not with fear-mongering.
Third: Three Challenges and Their Remedy through the Rabbaanie Methods Relying on the Innate Traits of the Age Group
The First Challenge — the limitedness of abstraction, so the child does not grasp abstract unseen meanings. The remedy: by harnessing the trait of curiosity — one of the most salient traits of this age — his question about the concrete is turned into an entry-point for acquainting him with the Creator, and the unseen is brought near through the nearest witnessed thing, so that his curiosity is satisfied with the truth before something else fills it.
The Second Challenge — corrupt reception from the surroundings, such as frightening with other than Allaah, and superstitions. The remedy: by harnessing the two traits of love of imitation and attachment to the parents, the parents are made a sound role model in speech and in emotional response, together with the screening of the contrary influence, so that the corrupt impression is replaced by the emulation of what is right.
The Third Challenge — the shortness of the attention span and the quickness of forgetting. The remedy: by harnessing the two traits of love of routine and love of story, the correct conception is implanted through a fixed daily repetition joined to a beloved song or story, so that it becomes fixed through repetition joined with delight, not through the lengthy lesson.
The Second Track: The Track of Applying Tazkiyah
First: The Foundational Grounding — Rules for Applying the Track for This Age Group
The First Rule: Tazkiyah at this age begins with implanting love and gentle affection, so that the child’s heart is opened to his Lord through love.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allaah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:165].
The point of evidence: He (glorified is He) made intensity of love for Him the highest description of the believers; this indicates that the first thing to be implanted in the heart is the love of Allaah.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Anas (may Allaah be pleased with him), who said: “The Prophet ﷺ used to come to us and say to a little brother of mine: ‘O Aboe 3Umayr, what has the little nightingale (nughayr) done?’”
The point of evidence: The Prophet’s ﷺ playful jesting with the small boy and his gentle affection toward him indicate that the entryway to the small child’s heart is love and gentle affection, not stern rebuke (zajr).
The fitrah-based rationale: Love was given precedence precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the intense attachment to the parents, the rapidity of emotional impressionability, and the love of gentle affection; the child’s heart is disposed to be drawn to whoever treats him tenderly, the verse of love makes it a foundation, and the Prophet’s ﷺ gentle affection toward the boy is a practical model. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: emotional attachment.
The Second Rule: The heart’s feelings are tied to tangible blessings, so that gratitude and love are implanted through what the child touches.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿But as for the favor of your Lord, report [it]﴾ [al-Duhaa 93:11].
The point of evidence: He commanded speaking of the blessing, and that engenders in the heart the witnessing of the Bestower, love of Him, and gratitude to Him.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Anas (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “Indeed, Allaah is pleased with the servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it.”
The point of evidence: He tied Allaah’s pleasure to the servant’s praising Him for the tangible blessing (eating and drinking); this indicates implanting gratitude in the heart through tangible blessings.
The fitrah-based rationale: The feelings were tied to the tangible precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the strong sense of ownership (“mine” and “yours”), the predominance of sensory perception, and curiosity toward what is given; the child perceives the blessing when he touches it, so this is made an entryway to love of the Bestower. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: the strong sense of ownership.
The Third Rule: The implanting of feelings is joined with the emotionally responsive role model, for the child acquires inner feeling by contagion, not by dictation.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allaah an excellent pattern﴾ [al-Ahzaab 33:21].
The point of evidence: He made the believers’ taking of His Messenger ﷺ as their model a foundation; and modeling in emotional response is more effective with the small child than dictation.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Anas (may Allaah be pleased with him): “I have never seen anyone more merciful toward children than the Messenger of Allaah ﷺ.”
The point of evidence: The description of his ﷺ mercy toward the young indicates that displaying merciful emotion before the child is an affective means of implanting.
The fitrah-based rationale: The emotionally responsive role model was adopted precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of imitation, emulation, and the rapidity of being impressed by what is witnessed; the child picks up the emotion of those around him before he understands their speech. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of imitation and emulation.
The Fourth Rule: The child’s heart is safeguarded from corrupt feelings, so that the religion is not linked with terror and harshness.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿So by mercy from Allaah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you﴾ [Aal 3Imraan 3:159].
The point of evidence: He made clear that rudeness and harshness drive hearts away; this indicates that implanting veneration in the heart is not accomplished through terrorizing.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Anas (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not repel.”
The point of evidence: He forbade repelling people in teaching and da3wah; this indicates the obligation to safeguard the learner’s heart from whatever repels.
The fitrah-based rationale: Safeguarding was emphasized precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the rapidity of emotional impressionability, the weak capacity to endure terror, and the child’s inclination to test boundaries; for morbid fear takes root quickly and is difficult to uproot. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: rapidity of emotional impressionability.
Second: Three Methods for Applying the Track, Each Method with Three Means
The First Method — concrete affective endearment: (a) linking blessings to the Bestower in a formula of love, such as saying “Allaah gave you this because He loves you”; (b) gentle affection and faith-based praise at obedience, such as saying “Maa shaa’ Allaah, Allaah loves the one who says Bismillaah”; (c) short stories that depict Allaah’s love for His righteous servants.
The Second Method — the emotionally responsive role model: (a) the parents’ displaying their joy at obedience before him; (b) displaying calm humility (khushoe3) at the remembrance of Allaah, by lowering the voice and by stillness; (c) sharing with him the feelings of gratitude at a blessing by saying “al-hamdu lillaah” with joy.
The Third Method — graduated affective habituation: (a) making the remembrance of Allaah (dhikr) part of the beloved daily routine; (b) songs of sound meaning with a joyful rhythm; (c) directing his emotions of anger and sadness gently toward tranquility, such as saying “Allaah loves the calm one.”
Third: Three Challenges and Their Remedy through the Rabbaanie Methods Relying on the Innate Traits of the Age Group
The First Challenge — linking the religion with excessive fear as a result of threatening with punishment. The remedy: by harnessing the two traits of attachment to the parents and rapid emotional impressionability, the side of love and hope is given predominance, and emotional safety with the parents is made a bridge to safety and intimacy with Allaah.
The Second Challenge — the weak grasp of abstract affective meanings such as love and awe. The remedy: by harnessing the two traits of the sense of ownership and the predominance of the sensory, the meaning is embodied through tangible blessings, and the feeling is tied to a concrete situation the child himself lives through.
The Third Challenge — the volatility of feelings and the quickness of emotional reaction. The remedy: by harnessing the two traits of love of routine and the sense of rhythm, sound feelings are entrenched through calm, regular repetition, and they are joined to a beloved song or dhikr that calms and steadies.
The Third Track: The Track of Applying the Upbringing of the Tongue
First: The Foundational Grounding — Rules for Applying the Track for This Age Group
The First Rule: The upbringing of the tongue at this age is an implanting of the vocabulary of faith in the growing linguistic stock.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿Have you not considered how Allaah presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky?﴾ [Ibraahiem 14:24].
The point of evidence: He likened the good word to the good tree, firmly rooted and fruitful in its branches; this indicates that implanting the good word early takes root and bears fruit.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Aboe Hurayrah (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “And the good word is charity.”
The point of evidence: He made the good word an act of worship and a charity; this indicates the merit of habituating the tongue to it and implanting it early.
The fitrah-based rationale: This was chosen precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the expansion of the linguistic stock, the love of imitation whereby he repeats what he hears, and the developing memory; the tongue acquires its vocabulary at this age rapidly and builds upon it. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: growth of the linguistic stock.
The Second Rule: The tongue is habituated to the remembrance of Allaah through repetition joined with the situation, not through imposition and obligation.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿So remember Me; I will remember you. And be grateful to Me and do not deny Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:152].
The point of evidence: He commanded remembrance and made Allaah’s remembrance of the servant its consequence; this indicates the great station of habituating the tongue to remembrance.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Samurah ibn Jundab (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “The dearest of speech to Allaah is four: Subhaan Allaah, al-hamdu lillaah, laa ilaaha illaa Allaah, and Allaahu akbar.”
The point of evidence: He specified the speech dearest to Allaah, and these are easy phrases that can be implanted upon the small child’s tongue in the situations of his day.
The fitrah-based rationale: Repetition joined with the situation was adopted precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of routine, the sense of rhythm, and the developing memory; the tongue becomes fixed upon what is repeated in a fixed, beloved context. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of routine and rhythm.
The Third Rule: The tongue’s utterance is tied to the role model, for the child says what he hears from those he loves in practical situations.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff 61:2].
The point of evidence: He censured the separation of word from deed; this indicates that the role model of speech must match the deed before the young.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of 3Umar ibn Abie Salamah (may Allaah be pleased with him), who said: the Messenger of Allaah ﷺ said to me: “O young lad, mention the name of Allaah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearest to you.”
The point of evidence: The Prophet ﷺ taught the lad the mention of Allaah’s name as speech joined to deed in a practical situation; this indicates teaching the tongue through the role model within the situation.
The fitrah-based rationale: Utterance was tied to the role model precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of imitation, emulation, and attachment to the role model; the child copies the wording of the one he loves. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of imitation.
The Fourth Rule: The tongue is safeguarded from foul utterance by screening its source and correcting it the moment it occurs.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿Allaah does not like the public mention of evil except by one who has been wronged﴾ [al-Nisaa’ 4:148].
The point of evidence: He made clear that Allaah does not love evil speech; this indicates the obligation to safeguard the tongue from foul talk.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Ibn Mas3oed (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “The believer is not one given to taunting, nor to cursing, nor one obscene, nor one foul-mouthed.”
The point of evidence: He negated of the believer obscenity and foulness of speech; this indicates the obligation to safeguard the tongue from them and to keep it free of them early.
The fitrah-based rationale: Safeguarding was given precedence precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of imitation whereby he repeats the bad word, the rapidity of being impressed by what is heard, and the child’s inclination to test boundaries; the foul word is picked up by mimicry before its meaning is understood. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of imitation and impressionability by what is heard.
Second: Three Methods for Applying the Track, Each Method with Three Means
The First Method — faith-based linguistic implanting: (a) incorporating the vocabulary of faith into his daily speech, such as “Bismillaah”, “al-hamdu lillaah”, and “maa shaa’ Allaah”; (b) tying the wording to its situation, such as mentioning Allaah’s name at mealtime and praising Him after it; (c) short songs that contain the remembrance of Allaah.
The Second Method — habituation through the verbal role model: (a) letting him hear his parents remembering Allaah in the situations of their day; (b) praising him when he utters the good word; (c) involving him in repeating simple collective remembrance.
The Third Method — preventive verbal safeguarding: (a) screening out the sources of foul speech from his surroundings; (b) correcting the erroneous utterance the moment it occurs, gently and with a good alternative; (c) cutting off reinforcement by not laughing at his bad utterance, lest it become fixed.
Third: Three Challenges and Their Remedy through the Rabbaanie Methods Relying on the Innate Traits of the Age Group
The First Challenge — the limitedness of the linguistic store and the difficulty of pronunciation. The remedy: by harnessing the two traits of the growth of the linguistic stock and the love of imitation, easy and concise phrases are selected and repeated within his hearing, so that he picks them up by mimicry and builds upon them.
The Second Challenge — picking up foul words from the surroundings. The remedy: by harnessing the knowledge of his rapid impressionability by what is heard, emptying is applied first by screening the source, then substitution with the good alternative, together with cutting off reinforcement by not paying attention and not laughing.
The Third Challenge — uttering the word without understanding its meaning. The remedy: by harnessing the two traits of the developing memory and the sense of rhythm, the word is joined to its tangible meaning within the situation and repeated in its context, until the meaning becomes associated with the word.
The Fourth Track: The Track of the Upbringing of the Limbs
First: The Foundational Grounding — Rules for Applying the Track for This Age Group
The First Rule: The upbringing of the limbs at this age is training by mimicry and preparation, not legal obligation; for there is no legal obligation before puberty.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿Allaah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:286].
The point of evidence: He (glorified is He) negated charging beyond capacity; this indicates observing the young child’s strength in the training of his limbs.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of 3Alie and 3aa’ishah (may Allaah be pleased with them both), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “The pen has been lifted from three: from the sleeper until he awakens, from the child until he reaches puberty, and from the insane until he comes to reason.”
The point of evidence: It lifted legal obligation from the child until puberty; this indicates that the work of the limbs in childhood is training and habituation, not binding obligation and accountability.
The fitrah-based rationale: It was made a training and not an obligation precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of imitation, the love of motor exploration, and imaginative play; the child mimics the movement of those around him for delight, not out of compliance. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of imitation through mimicry.
The Second Rule: Worship is implanted in the limbs through the visible role model and motor participation.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast therein﴾ [Taa Haa 20:132].
The point of evidence: He commanded enjoining prayer upon the family and patience therein; this indicates habituating the family, including the young, to it gradually.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Maalik ibn al-Huwayrith (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “Pray as you have seen me pray.”
The point of evidence: The Prophet ﷺ made the performance of prayer contingent upon the visual mimicry of his action; this indicates that the limbs are trained through the visible role model.
The fitrah-based rationale: The visible role model was adopted precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of motor exploration, the love of imitation, and attachment to the parents; the child mimics the movement he sees from the one he loves. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: love of motor exploration and mimicry.
The Third Rule: The work of the limbs is joined with endearment and encouragement, so that the deed becomes associated with delight, not with aversion.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿Allaah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185].
The point of evidence: He (glorified is He) informed that He intends ease for His servants; this indicates easing the training of the limbs and not making it burdensome for the young.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of Aboe Hurayrah (may Allaah be pleased with him), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “Indeed, the religion is ease, and no one strains against the religion but that it overcomes him.”
The point of evidence: He described the religion as ease and forbade contending with it; this indicates that habituating the limbs is done with gentleness and gradation.
The fitrah-based rationale: The deed was joined with endearment precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the positive responsiveness to encouragement, the love of routine, and the child’s inclination to test boundaries; praise consolidates the deed, while stern rebuke repels from it. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: positive responsiveness to encouragement.
The Fourth Rule: The child is safeguarded from the fixing of the bad deed upon his limbs, and his motor energy is directed toward what is beneficial.
The evidence from the Book: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart — about all those [one] will be questioned﴾ [al-Israa’ 17:36].
The point of evidence: He affirmed responsibility for the limbs and senses; this indicates attentiveness to regulating and directing their movement early.
The evidence from the Sunnah: the hadieth of 3Abd Allaah ibn 3Amr ibn al-3aas (may Allaah be pleased with them both), traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: “Command your children to pray when they are seven years old, and discipline them for it when they are ten, and separate them in their beds.”
The point of evidence: It fixed the commencement of commanding prayer at seven, and what precedes it is preparation and habituation of the limbs; this indicates gradation in directing them.
The fitrah-based rationale: Safeguarding and direction were given precedence precisely because of the convergence of traits at this age: the love of motor exploration, the child’s inclination to test boundaries, and the love of routine; his motor energy is dissipated if it is not directed. The most fitting name for the governing trait is: motor energy and boundary-testing.
Second: Three Methods for Applying the Track, Each Method with Three Means
The First Method — training by mimicry: (a) his imitating the parents in the movements of prayer by way of endearment; (b) involving him in a symbolic wudoe’; (c) repeating movements joined with remembrance, such as raising the hands in supplication.
The Second Method — habituation through the visible role model: (a) taking him along to the places of worship according to his capacity; (b) his seeing the parents in obedience daily; (c) entrusting to him a small, beneficial motor task, such as handing over the mushaf and arranging the place of prayer.
The Third Method — endearment and motor direction: (a) praise and encouragement at the good deed; (b) placing the deed within a beloved daily routine; (c) directing his motor energy of running and climbing toward what is beneficial, while tying it to gratitude, such as saying “Allaah gave you a strong body.”
Third: Three Challenges and Their Remedy through the Rabbaanie Methods Relying on the Innate Traits of the Age Group
The First Challenge — the shortness of concentration and the inability to endure lengthy worship. The remedy: by harnessing the trait of love of motor exploration, the act is divided into short, beloved movements, and it is made closer to organized play than to the lengthy lesson.
The Second Challenge — imitating the bad deed from the surroundings. The remedy: by harnessing the trait of love of imitation, the motor role model is regulated and the bad model is screened off, and the good deed is put in its place through mimicry.
The Third Challenge — resistance and boundary-testing. The remedy: by harnessing the trait of positive responsiveness to encouragement, encouragement and praise are given predominance over stern rebuke, and limited choices are offered that give him a sense of will within what is required.
The Detailed Innate Characteristics Specific to the Age Stage from Birth to Two Years, and How to Direct Them Pedagogically for the Veneration of Allaah and the Governance of the Deeds of the Hearts
In this stage the child passes through rapidly succeeding phases of the fitrah, bodily and psychological, while he is not yet legally accountable; hence the treatment of his characteristics along the four tracks (tasfiyah, tazkiyah, the upbringing of the tongue, and the upbringing of the limbs) is directed to the educator (murabbie) himself, by which he prepares around the child the environment of faith saturated with the remembrance and veneration of Allaah, so that his fitrah is imprinted with tranquility and faith from his earliest days. This stage is divided, according to the bodily and psychological fitrah, into four groups:
The Age Group from Birth to Two Years
Applying the discipline of time in this age group through the four tracks (the educator embodies it and directs it):
Through tasfiyah: It is established in the educator’s awareness that regulating the infant’s time begins with regulating his rhythm (sleep, feeding, and waking at closely spaced, regular times), so that his body grows up upon order before understanding.
Through tazkiyah: Tranquility is implanted through the regularity of his day; the fixed rhythm engenders serenity in the infant, while chaos engenders in him disturbance and anxiety.
Through the upbringing of the tongue: He is given to hear the sounds of the calm hours: recitation and remembrance at bedtime, and gentle words at waking, so that regulated time becomes associated for him with stillness.
Through the upbringing of the limbs: He is habituated to regular times of sleep and feeding, and kept away from the disruption of night and day, so that his bodily rhythm takes shape upon the order that will ease his self-discipline later.
Applying the virtue of sincere counsel in this age group through the four tracks (the educator embodies it and directs it):
Through tasfiyah: It is established in the educator’s awareness that counseling this age group is by state, not by speech; the child picks up the tone and the emotion before the word, so the educator takes care to be a calm, loving role model in everything the child sees of him.
Through tazkiyah: Tranquility and love are implanted in the child’s heart through tenderness, touch, and the gentle voice, so that his emotional life grows up upon security — the foundation by which he will later accept direction and counsel.
Through the upbringing of the tongue: The child is given to hear the good word, supplication, and remembrance in a soft, tender voice, so that he grows familiar with the melody of gentleness before he comprehends the meaning, and direction becomes associated for him with mildness, not with harshness.
Through the upbringing of the limbs: His behavior is directed by gentle removal and by offering an alternative, not by stern rebuke and violence, and he sees the excellent example in his parents’ conduct and their treatment of others, so that his inner nature takes shape upon gentleness and mildness.
The Beautiful Names of Allaah and Their Pedagogical Application in This Age Group
The veneration of Allaah is built in the child’s heart upon knowledge of His beautiful names and their meanings; and in this age group the infant receives the meanings of these names through his parents’ treatment of him before he can comprehend them, so the educator embodies them and directs them in his care. These comprehensive names are a foundation upon which the explanation of the names for the subsequent age groups is built.
The Name of Allaah: al-Rahmaan
The Meaning and Its Three Modes of Signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Rahmaan” is on the pattern of “fa3laan”, which denotes vastness, fullness, and intensification; by full correspondence it thus signifies the essence of Allaah described with a vast, immense mercy that has encompassed all things; so He is the Possessor of the all-embracing mercy toward all His creation in this world.
Indication by inclusion (tadammun): The name includes the affirmation of the divine Essence and the affirmation of the attribute of mercy subsisting in it; both parts are intended by the name, and neither of them can be separated from the other.
Indication by implication (iltizaam): It necessitates, beyond its wording, perfections belonging to Allaah: life (for mercy is the attribute of a living one), will, power, and knowledge (for He shows mercy to whom He wills, however He wills, with knowledge and power); and it necessitates effects within creation: provision, giving, well-being, and forgiveness.
The scholarly and exhortative explanation: Ibn al-Qayyim established that the names of Allaah signify by these three modes of indication, and that “al-Rahmaan” signifies the vast mercy that encompasses all things. Reflect — O educator (murabbie) — on how His mercy has encompassed you and your child: the pregnancy is a mercy, the delivery is a mercy, the freely flowing milk is a mercy; indeed, your very tenderness toward your child is a trace of His mercy that He has deposited in your heart. For in the hadieth it is related that Allaah made mercy one hundred parts, of which He sent down a single part by which the whole of creation shows mercy to one another (Agreed upon: al-Bukhaarie and Muslim). What, then, do you reckon of the ninety-nine parts stored up for His servants on the Day of Resurrection?
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): In this name lies the greatest encouragement, for His mercy has preceded His anger and has encompassed all things, so that none despairs of it save one gone astray. And in it lies a warning: that His special, complete mercy belongs to the pious believers, and that He is al-Rahmaan while also being severe in punishment; so let no one be deluded by its vastness into growing bold in disobeying Him.
The pedagogical application through the four tracks within this age group (the educator embodies it and directs it):
Through purging (tasfiyah): The educator couples every blessing he presents to the infant with its attribution to Allaah, al-Rahmaan — in word within its hearing and in heart within his own soul — thereby inscribing in its surroundings that the source of every mercy is Allaah. He makes the names “Allaah” and “al-Rahmaan” among the first things to reach the child’s hearing, so that through repetition it becomes fixed within its inner being that behind its mother’s tenderness lies a greater mercy: the mercy of al-Rahmaan (this is applied to the trait of attachment to the mother).
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): The infant is immersed in tenderness and reassurance, so that its emotional life develops upon security rather than fear; for its tazkiyah at this stage is that it experience mercy in a tangible, sensory way and grow familiar with it, so that it becomes fixed in its innate disposition (fitrah) that its Lord is Rahmaan. The educator spares it the harshness and shouting that sow fear and distort its conception of mercy. By way of encouragement, it is bound to the love of the Merciful One who shows it mercy; and by way of warning — addressed to the educator — he must beware of harshness, for in the hadieth it is said: “Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy” (Agreed upon: al-Bukhaarie and Muslim).
Through the upbringing of the tongue: The mother lets her child hear the words “Allaah” and “al-Rahmaan”, the basmalah, and the remembrance of Allaah, and she lets it hear al-Faatihah, which contains ﴿The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Faatihah 1:3], so that once it reaches the age of discernment its tongue develops upon what its ear has grown accustomed to; for the tongue utters that upon which the hearing has been reared.
Through the upbringing of the limbs: The educator is merciful in his conduct — in carrying the child, in touching it, and in treating it gently — so that the child receives mercy in deed before word; and as it grows, it is habituated to the effects of mercy: gentleness toward animals and kindness toward the young, so that it grows up knowing that whomever al-Rahmaan has shown mercy shows mercy to His creation — as encouragement toward the mercy Allaah grants the merciful.
The Name of Allaah: al-Rahiem
The meaning and its three indications:
Indication by correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Rahiem” is on the pattern “fa3iel”, which signifies the firm establishment and permanence of the attribute. If “al-Rahmaan” signifies the vastness of mercy in itself, then “al-Rahiem” signifies, by correspondence, its actual delivery and implementation in those who receive mercy, especially the believers (building upon the meaning of “al-Rahmaan” set out above).
Indication by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and of the active attribute of mercy that reaches its recipients.
Indication by implication (iltizaam): It necessitates — like al-Rahmaan — life, will, power, and knowledge, and it necessitates the arrival of mercy’s effects: forgiveness, divine enablement (tawfieq), guidance, and gentleness toward the believers in particular. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿And ever is He, to the believers, Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzaab 33:43].
The scholarly and exhortative explanation: The pairing of “al-Rahmaan al-Rahiem” thus combines the vastness of mercy and its delivery. He is the Rahmaan of this world and the Hereafter and the Rahiem of them both: with His general mercy He shows mercy to all His creation, and He singles out the believers with a special mercy in both abodes. How immense, then, is the portion of one who enters into His special mercy through faith and obedience!
Encouragement and warning: Encouragement: that the believer is singled out for a special mercy, so let him aspire to it through obedience. And warning: that this special mercy is not attained by wishful thinking but by faith and works; and whoever is deprived of it by his turning away has been deprived of the greatest portion.
The pedagogical application through the four tracks within this age group (the educator embodies it and directs it):
Through purging (tasfiyah): The educator establishes — by coupling care with this name — that Allaah’s mercy toward the child is not merely general but reaches it specifically, thereby inscribing in its surroundings that Allaah shows mercy to it in particular, not that it is one anonymous soul lost in the crowd.
Through tazkiyah: There is implanted in the child — in a sensory way — the sweetness of being shown mercy and being loved, so that its emotional life develops upon aspiring to Allaah’s mercy and His love, through tenderness that is continuous, not intermittent.
Through the upbringing of the tongue: The mother repeats within its hearing “al-Rahiem” coupled with “al-Rahmaan” in the basmalah, in al-Faatihah, and in remembrance, so that it grows familiar with their pairing and its tongue develops upon joining the two together.
Through the upbringing of the limbs: The educator conveys his mercy to the child in action that is continuous, not intermittent (at the appointed times of its feeding and its rest), so that it experiences the meaning of mercy that truly arrives; and as it grows, it is habituated to conveying kindness to others in deed, not contenting itself with mere feeling.
The Name of Allaah: al-Razzaaq
The meaning and its three indications:
Indication by correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Razzaaq” is on the pattern “fa33aal”, which signifies intensity and abundance; thus by correspondence it signifies the Essence of Allaah as described by the abundance of provision and its vastness for all creation. He it is who created the provisions, apportioned them, and delivered them.
Indication by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and of the attribute of repeated, vast provision.
Indication by implication (iltizaam): It necessitates power and knowledge (He knows the needs of His creation and is able to provide for them), as well as life, self-sufficiency, and generosity; and it necessitates His exclusive claim to provision, so that there is no provider besides Him. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is Allaah who is the [continual] Provider, the firm possessor of strength﴾ [al-Dhaariyaat 51:58].
The scholarly and exhortative explanation: All provision is in His hand, from the milk in the breast to the fruit on the tree. Reflect on how He conveyed His provision to your unborn and newborn child before it could ever ask, preparing for it in its mother’s breast a nourishment that neither the child nor its mother could ever manufacture. Whoever places his trust in al-Razzaaq is relieved of all anxiety over provision.
Encouragement and warning: Encouragement: that whoever relies upon al-Razzaaq and is mindful of Him, He provides for him from where he does not expect. And warning: that attachment to the means while neglecting the One who ordains them, or seeking provision through the unlawful, amounts to claiming independence from al-Razzaaq and thinking ill of Him.
The pedagogical application through the four tracks within this age group (the educator embodies it and directs it):
Through purging (tasfiyah): The mother attributes the child’s provision — her milk and its food — to Allaah, al-Razzaaq, within its hearing, so that it is established in its surroundings that the true Feeder is Allaah, not the hand that offers the food.
Through tazkiyah: There is implanted in the child — as it grows and its awareness develops — gratitude to Allaah, the One who feeds, so that its emotional life develops upon thanking al-Razzaaq rather than mere attachment to food.
Through the upbringing of the tongue: The mother instills within its hearing the mention of Allaah’s name before food and the praise of Him after it, so that its tongue develops upon remembering al-Razzaaq at the moment of receiving His provision.
Through the upbringing of the limbs: The child is gradually habituated to the etiquettes of eating (saying the tasmiyah and eating with the right hand) and to avoiding wastefulness, out of gratitude to al-Razzaaq; and as it grows older, its being fed is linked to its feeding of others.
The Name of Allaah: al-Khaaliq
The meaning and its three indications:
Indication by correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Khaaliq” signifies by correspondence the Essence of Allaah as described by the attribute of creating — that is, bringing things into existence and determining them without any prior model; He is the Bringer-into-being, the Originator, the Determiner.
Indication by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and of the attribute of creation subsisting in it.
Indication by implication (iltizaam): It necessitates complete power, knowledge, will, and life; and it necessitates His exclusive claim to creation, so that there is no creator besides Him. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allaah?﴾ [Faatir 35:3]. It likewise necessitates that everything besides Him is created, subject to His lordship, and utterly in need of Him.
The scholarly and exhortative explanation: Reflect, then, on the creation of your newborn: a sperm-drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bones clothed with flesh, then brought forth as a well-proportioned creature endowed with hearing, sight, and a heart; ﴿So blessed is Allaah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu’minoen 23:14]. Whoever knows that Allaah created him knows that he is owned by Him and is bound to single Him out in worship and obedience.
Encouragement and warning: Encouragement: that the Creator who so wondrously originated your creation is more merciful to you than your own self and more knowing of what truly benefits you, so trust in His management. And warning: that whoever disobeys his Creator and waxes arrogant has denied the right of the One who brought him forth from nothing, and to Him is his return and his final destination.
The pedagogical application through the four tracks within this age group (the educator embodies it and directs it):
Through purging (tasfiyah): The educator establishes in the child’s surroundings that Allaah created it and created everything around it, thereby inscribing the first meanings of lordship (ruboebiyyah): that there is a Creator of all things, and that nothing comes into existence without one who brings it into being.
Through tazkiyah: There is implanted in the child — as its awareness develops — wonder at Allaah’s creation and love for its Creator, so that its emotional life develops upon veneration of the originating Maker.
Through the upbringing of the tongue: It is made to hear the verses concerning creation and the remembrances connected to it, and once it can speak it is taught that “Allaah created me”, so that its tongue develops upon attributing creation to Allaah.
Through the upbringing of the limbs: The child is directed — as it grows — to contemplate the creatures of Allaah and to treat them gently because they are Allaah’s creation, so that its limbs act in accordance with the veneration of the Creator.
The First Age Group: From Birth to Six Months
In this stage the child is dominated by sensory reception, attachment to the mother, responsiveness to sounds and faces, and the need for reassurance. Among its innate traits are:
1. The innate attachment to the mother — to her voice, her scent, and her embrace.
The method of direction: The mother takes care to be, while nursing and carrying her child, engaged in the remembrance of Allaah and at peace, so that from its very first attachment the infant absorbs the tranquility that is coupled with the remembrance of Allaah.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator couples the child’s care with the attribution of every blessing to Allaah, thereby establishing in its surroundings that Allaah is the Bestower of blessings, even if the child does not yet grasp this. He repeats this so that it becomes a foundation in its earliest environment.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The mother immerses her child in tenderness coupled with the remembrance of Allaah, so that from its attachment to her it absorbs a serenity whose source is faith. She intends thereby that its attachment grow toward the love of Allaah.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The mother lets her child hear, while nursing and carrying it, the words of the tasmiyah and of remembrance, gently, so that it grows familiar with her voice coupled with the remembrance of Allaah. She keeps this up at every encounter.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The mother embraces her child and touches it tenderly while supplicating for it, so that its bodily care is coupled with the atmosphere of faith. She makes this her constant habit in caring for it.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator invests the child’s attachment to him so as to make the first thing imprinted upon its innate disposition that the source of security and provision is Allaah, thereby founding the leadership of its soul upon tawhied from the cradle.
Through leading the emotions: The educator receives the child’s attachment with calm, measured tenderness, thereby implanting a serenity whose source is faith rather than anxiety, and directing the emotion of its attachment to grow toward the love of Allaah.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator keeps present in his care the intention of raising a servant for Allaah, not for himself, so that he nurtures the child’s attachment to become the starting point of an attachment to Allaah, not a means of binding the child in servitude to himself.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes the child’s attachment to him a first bridge toward a love that ascends by degrees toward Allaah, His Messenger, and the people of faith, so that it grows up upon loyalty to goodness and its people.
Through patience: The educator bears patiently the demands of the child attached to him and does not grow irritated; by his patience he implants security, and he paves the way for gradually habituating it to patience during his absence.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator counsels this child that is attached to him by his state, not by his speech, being a calm and loving example, and he implants the first guidance through tenderness, not through stern rebuke (zajr).
Through regulating time: The educator organizes the times of caressing the child and of answering its attachment in a steady rhythm, so that its security is coupled with the regularity of its day, not with its chaos.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator protects the child’s attachment from deviating into an anxious attachment that Satan would exploit through whispering (waswaas), making it instead a sound attachment whose point of reference is tranquility in Allaah.
2. Responsiveness to sounds and turning toward them.
The method of direction: Care is taken that the first thing to strike its hearing at its birth be the adhaan, then the Qur’aan and remembrance, so that the cadences of revelation are imprinted upon its earliest auditory disposition.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator takes care that the first thing to strike the child’s hearing be the adhaan and then the Qur’aan, so that its hearing is founded upon the sounds of revelation. He repeats them so that they become imprinted upon its innate disposition.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The educator couples wholesome sounds with feelings of reassurance, so that in the child’s inner life the sound of remembrance becomes bound to serenity. He intends to implant an early intimacy with the speech of Allaah.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The educator recites the Qur’aan and remembrance abundantly, in an audible voice, near the child. He makes this part of his day.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The educator gently directs the child toward the source of the wholesome sound, so that it turns toward it. He repeats this, binding its movement to goodness.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator makes the first thing to which the child’s ear responds the sound of the adhaan and the Qur’aan, thereby founding its hearing upon the guidance of revelation by which the soul is led.
Through leading the emotions: The educator couples wholesome sounds with comfort and reassurance, so that the child’s responsiveness develops coupled with an emotion of intimacy with the speech of Allaah, not aversion.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): In letting it hear the Qur’aan and remembrance, the educator seeks the Face of Allaah and the child’s servitude to Him, not mere entertainment or boasting.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The educator endears to the child’s hearing the sounds of remembrance and of its people, and keeps it far from the sounds of idle amusement and disobedience, so that it grows familiar with what Allaah loves.
Through patience: The educator perseveres in letting it hear what is wholesome and does not hasten after fruit, patient with repetition until the response takes root in its innate disposition.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator directs the child’s hearing by his state, letting it hear what is wholesome with gentleness and by example, and he makes his counsel to it consist in selecting what strikes its hearing.
Through regulating time: The educator seizes the child’s moments of clear wakefulness to let it hear the adhaan and the Qur’aan, thus investing the most beneficial time for the imprinting of revelation.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator guards the child’s hearing from the sounds of falsehood that Satan adorns, and does not enable the enemy to plant in its ears what would bar it from Allaah.
3. Visual tracking of faces and objects.
The method of direction: It is surrounded by the faces of the people of righteousness and love and by calm, natural scenes, together with the naming of things and the praising of Allaah for the blessing of sight in its presence.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator surrounds the child with calm, natural scenes that point to the handiwork of Allaah, and he names them for it. He makes the first things its eye falls upon the signs of creation.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The educator couples whatever beauty the child sees with the praise of Allaah, so that its first observations become bound to gratitude toward the Creator. He intends to implant an early veneration.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The educator praises Allaah for the blessing of sight in front of the child and names what it sees. He repeats this at every scene.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The educator moves before the child whatever draws its gaze toward the wholesome, so that it tracks it. He repeats this, binding its sight to goodness.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator makes the first things the child’s eye tracks scenes that point to the greatness of the Creator, thereby founding its sight upon looking at what leads to Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator couples whatever beauty the child beholds with praise and cheerfulness, so that the emotion of admiration develops connected to the veneration of its Maker, not to the mere thing itself.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): In directing the child’s gaze toward the wholesome, the educator intends its servitude to Allaah and its being acquainted with Him, not adornment and boasting.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The educator directs the child’s gaze toward what Allaah loves, such as the mushaf and the people of righteousness, and turns it away from what He detests, so that its sight grows familiar with goodness.
Through patience: The educator repeats the directing of the child’s gaze with patience and gentleness and does not coerce it, until it becomes accustomed to tracking what is beneficial.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator directs the child’s gaze with gentleness and by example, not by coercion, counseling it by his state through presenting to it what is beneficial rather than what is harmful.
Through regulating time: The educator chooses the child’s moments of clarity for directing its gaze toward what is beneficial, and during its times of rest he keeps from it whatever would scatter its attention.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator protects the child’s sight from the sights that Satan adorns, thereby founding the lowering of the gaze from what harms from its earliest days.
4. The first social smile.
The method of direction: Its smile is met with cheerfulness, supplication for it, and the praise of Allaah, so that its first social contact is coupled with joy bound to Allaah.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator receives the child’s smile in a way that establishes that joy is a blessing from Allaah, praising Him for it. He makes its first contact coupled with the remembrance of the Bestower.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The educator meets its smile with love and cheerfulness coupled with supplication, so that its joy becomes bound to an atmosphere of love for the sake of Allaah. He intends to implant a faith-filled gladness.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The educator supplicates for the child and praises Allaah in an audible voice at its smile. He repeats this whenever it smiles.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The educator caresses the child and exchanges cheerfulness with it through his face and his tender touch, so that its contact is coupled with gentleness. He keeps this up constantly.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator receives the child’s smile in a way that binds it to goodness, thereby establishing that the occasions of joy are the occasions of obedience, so that its soul is led to rejoice in the truth.
Through leading the emotions: The educator meets the child’s cheerfulness with measured cheerfulness coupled with supplication, thereby implanting a balanced, faith-filled gladness, not frivolity.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By caressing the child the educator intends to win its heart over to goodness for the sake of Allaah, not to ingratiate himself for some worldly aim.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The educator sets the exchange of cheerfulness between himself and the child within an atmosphere of love for the sake of Allaah, so that its love for the people of goodness, and its cheerfulness toward them, take shape.
Through patience: The educator caresses the child and exchanges cheerfulness with it with constancy and with patience in its care, so that its sense of intimacy becomes firm and it does not shy away.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator exchanges cheerfulness with the child as a tender example, so that his first counsel is a beaming face, not a scowl that repels.
Through regulating time: The educator maintains regular times for caressing and cheerfulness, so that the child’s intimacy is made firm by the regularity of their meeting, not by its intermittency.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator guards the child’s gladness from being channeled into frivolity that Satan adorns, binding its joy to what is wholesome, not to falsehood.
5. Soothing through tender touch and being carried.
The method of direction: It is soothed with a tender embrace while the mu3awwidhaat (the soerahs of seeking refuge) and the remembrances are recited over it, so that its reassurance is coupled with the speech of Allaah, not with heedlessness.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator keeps present that serenity is a blessing Allaah sends down, so he seeks it through its means together with remembrance. He makes the soothing of the child coupled with the truth that reassurance comes from Allaah.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The educator soothes the child with tenderness while keeping present the love of Allaah, so that its reassurance becomes bound to the atmosphere of faith, not heedlessness. He intends to implant a faith-filled serenity.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The educator recites the mu3awwidhaat and the remembrances over the child when soothing it. He keeps this up every time.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The educator carries the child and pats it gently while softly breathing the remembrance over it. He makes this his method of soothing.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator makes the soothing of the child by touch coupled with the meaning that serenity descends from Allaah, thereby establishing that the point of reference for reassurance is He, glorified is He.
Through leading the emotions: The educator calms the child’s agitation with a tender, quiet touch coupled with remembrance, thereby implanting a faith-filled serenity that regulates its feelings.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): In soothing the child the educator intends mercy toward it, seeking the Face of Allaah, not merely silencing it so that he himself may rest.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes his tender touch a translation of a mercy that Allaah loves, so that the child grows up knowing that tenderness is coupled with goodness and its people.
Through patience: The educator bears patiently the repeated soothing of the child without irritation, hoping for reward, thereby implanting security in the child and training his own soul in forbearance.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator soothes the child with gentleness and forbearance as an example, counseling it by his state that its distress is to be met with softness, not severity.
Through regulating time: The educator regulates the child’s times of sleep and food so that its need for soothing diminishes, thus warding off its agitation by regulating its rhythm.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator takes care not to soothe the child with what would distract it from goodness or open the door to a bad habit that Satan would exploit later.
6. Crying as a language for expressing need.
The method of direction: Its crying is met with mercy, patience, and supplication for it, and irritation is avoided; for mercy toward the child is part of venerating Allaah’s command concerning it.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator keeps present that mercy toward the child is part of venerating Allaah’s command concerning it, so he shows it mercy and does not grow irritated. He establishes an environment whose foundation is mercy.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The educator meets the child’s crying with patience, tenderness, and supplication for it, so that its need becomes bound to mercy coupled with faith. He intends to implant security.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The educator supplicates for the child and remembers Allaah at its crying with calm speech. He repeats this, soothing it.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The educator hastens to fulfill the child’s need with gentleness and a tender touch. He makes this his habit, without irritation.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator reads the child’s crying as a language of need, not as obstinacy, and answers it with wisdom, thereby establishing that the fulfillment of needs comes from Allaah alone.
Through leading the emotions: The educator meets the child’s crying with calm and mercy, not agitation, thereby steadying the emotional atmosphere and implanting reassurance.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): When answering the child’s crying, the educator keeps present the hope of reward with Allaah, not merely being rid of an annoyance.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes his mercy toward the child’s crying an act of compliance with the mercy toward the young that Allaah loves, so that the child is reared upon the value of mercy.
Through patience: The educator bears the child’s crying patiently and is not harsh, hoping for reward; thus he trains his own soul in forbearance and implants security in the child.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator receives the child’s crying with gentleness, not violence, as an example, counseling it by his state with mercy and forbearance.
Through regulating time: The educator checks on the child’s needs at their regular times, whether hunger or sleep, thus forestalling the crying by regulating its schedule.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator bewares lest his vexation at the crying drag him into a harshness adorned by anger and by Satan, and so he stands guard over mercy.
7. The sucking reflex and breastfeeding.
The method of direction: Nursing is opened with the tasmiyah and set within an atmosphere of serenity, so that the child grows up upon the truth that blessings are opened with the name of Allaah.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator establishes that provision is from Allaah, and so he opens the nursing with the tasmiyah. He makes the first blessing the child receives coupled with the name of Allaah.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The mother nurses her child in serenity, remembrance, and love, so that its first nourishment becomes bound to the atmosphere of faith. She intends thereby gratitude to Allaah for the blessing of provision.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The mother mentions Allaah’s name before nursing and praises Him afterward in an audible voice. She keeps this up every time.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The mother sets the nursing in calm and reassurance, far from idle distraction. She adheres to this as a constant practice.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The mother opens the child’s nursing with the tasmiyah, thereby establishing that the first provision it receives is from Allaah, so that its soul is led to attribute blessings to Him.
Through leading the emotions: The mother nurses her child in serenity and love coupled with remembrance, so that its nourishment becomes bound to an emotion of security and faith-filled intimacy.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The mother keeps present in her nursing the intention of fulfilling Allaah’s right in the upbringing of her child, so that she makes it an act of worship, not a mere habit.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The mother makes the blessing of nursing a gateway for later acquainting the child with the love of al-Razzaaq and gratitude to Him, so that its love for Allaah, the Bestower, takes shape.
Through patience: The mother bears the hardship of nursing patiently and hopes for reward, thereby training her own soul in patience in obedience and fulfilling her child’s right.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The mother fulfills her child’s right to nursing as an example hoping for reward, so that her counsel to it takes the form of giving and kindness, not of reproachful favor.
Through regulating time: The mother organizes the times of nursing at close, regular intervals, thereby regulating the child’s rhythm and preserving her own time.
Through knowing the enemies: The mother takes care that the nursing take place in purity and calm, far from the occasions of heedlessness, so that she opens no door for Satan into the child’s nourishment and its atmosphere.
8. The innate need for reassurance and security.
The method of direction: It is provided an atmosphere of serenity and the stability of routine, with the home kept alive with the recitation of the Qur’aan; for in a home thriving with remembrance its innate disposition finds rest.
First: Treating it through tasfiyah
The educator establishes that security is a blessing from Allaah, and so he provides the child a stable environment thriving with the Qur’aan. He makes its dwelling coupled with the remembrance of Allaah.
Second: Treating it through tazkiyah
The educator fills the child’s surroundings with serenity and love for the sake of Allaah, so that its innate disposition finds rest. He intends that it grow up upon faith-based security.
Third: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the tongue
The educator recites the Qur’aan abundantly in the home within the child’s hearing. He makes it a daily habit.
Fourth: Treating it through tarbiyah — the upbringing of the limbs
The educator provides the child the stability of routine and a safe embrace. He maintains this constantly in its care.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator provides the child a stable environment thriving with the remembrance of Allaah, thereby establishing that the true source of security is Allaah, so that its soul is led to Him.
Through leading the emotions: The educator fills the child’s surroundings with serenity and love, so that its emotional life develops upon faith-based reassurance, not anxiety.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): In preparing security for the child the educator intends to prepare it as a servant at rest in Allaah, not mere worldly comfort.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal: The educator binds the child’s security to the love of Allaah and the presence of His remembrance, so that it grows up knowing that serenity lies in loyalty to Allaah and His people.
Through patience: The educator persists in providing security for the child with steadfastness and patience in its care, so that security takes root in its innate disposition.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator provides security for the child as a steady example, counseling it by his state to be itself a source of reassurance, not of fear.
Through regulating time: The educator makes the child’s daily routine firm, so that its security takes root through the regularity of its times, not through their fluctuation.
