Through knowing the enemies: The educator is wary lest the child imitate from him or from those around him an evil that Satan adorns, thereby guarding his example and his environment.
4. The Beginning of Simple Imaginative Play.
Method of direction: His play is directed toward imitating good (symbolic prayer, feeding a doll), so that his imagination is nurtured upon the meanings of worship and excellence (ihsaan).
First: Addressing it through purging
The educator directs the child’s play toward imitating good. He establishes that good play is loved by Allaah.
Second: Addressing it through purification
The educator rejoices at the child’s play in good with love. He intends to bind his imagination to what is good.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing — formation of the tongue
The educator teaches the child to say remembrance in his play, such as the invocation of Allaah’s name over his doll. He repeats that.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing — formation of the limbs
The educator acts out with the child the deeds of good, such as a symbolic prayer and feeding a doll. He persists in that.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through the leadership of the soul and the seeking of knowledge: The educator directs the child’s imaginative play toward imitating good, thereby establishing that his imagination is directed toward that by which the soul is led to Allaah.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator rejoices at the child’s play in good with love, thereby instilling an emotion of inclination toward what is good.
Through sincerity: By directing the child’s play, the educator intends to raise him upon love of good for the sake of Allaah, not merely for amusement.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator acts out with the child the deeds of good that Allaah loves, such as a symbolic prayer and feeding, and keeps him away from acting out evil, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience: The educator shares in the child’s purposeful play with patience and perseverance, so that his inclination toward good is made firm.
Through sincere counsel: The educator shares in the child’s purposeful play as a role model, so that he counsels him by his state to incline toward good in his amusement.
Through the regulation of time: The educator sets aside purposeful, regular times of play, so that his inclination toward good is made firm at a fruitful time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator guards the child’s play from imitating evil and violence that Satan adorns, thereby making his imagination in good.
5. The Emergence of Will and Independence and the Word “No.”
Method of direction: His budding will is respected and directed gently, and limited good choices are made available to him, so that his personality grows within the framework of good, neither suppression nor disorder.
First: Addressing it through purging
The educator respects the child’s will and directs it gently toward what is good. He establishes that good is a beloved choice.
Second: Addressing it through purification
The educator meets the child’s will with love and forbearance conjoined with tranquility. He intends to bind his will to good rather than suppression.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing — formation of the tongue
The educator makes the good beloved to the child with gentle speech conjoined with remembrance. He repeats that.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing — formation of the limbs
The educator makes available to the child limited good choices that he practices. He keeps to that.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through the leadership of the soul and the seeking of knowledge: The educator respects the child’s budding will and directs it gently toward good, thereby establishing a will by which the soul is led to the obedience of Allaah.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator meets the child’s obstinacy with forbearance rather than harshness, thereby restraining the agitation of his will and transforming it into a balanced inclination toward good.
Through sincerity: By directing the child’s will, the educator intends to raise him upon preferring what pleases Allaah, not to break his will for its own sake.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child that he should will what Allaah loves and habituates him to abandon what He detests, so that his will is raised upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience: The educator is patient with the child’s obstinacy and directs him gently without suppression or spoiling, thereby raising his own self upon forbearance.
Through sincere counsel: The educator directs the child’s obstinacy gently, without suppression or spoiling, as a role model, so that he counsels him by his state with forbearance and moderation.
Through the regulation of time: The educator selects the times of the child’s calm to direct him, not the times of his tension, thereby containing his obstinacy at a suitable time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator directs the child’s will toward good, so he does not leave it to follow every caprice that Satan adorns, and he habituates him to restraining himself.
6. Fits of Anger and Agitation.
Method of direction: His anger is met with calm and tenderness rather than violence, and he is soothed gently, so that he learns by his innate disposition that serenity is better than anger.
First: Addressing it through purging
The educator (murabbie) establishes that tranquillity is a good that Allaah loves, so he meets the child’s anger with calm. He repeats this.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator meets the child’s anger with forbearance and tenderness, not harshness, so he calms down. He intends to teach him tranquillity.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child a calming word, such as a simplified seeking of refuge (isti3aadhah), when he is angry. He repeats this.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator calms the child gently with a tender touch when he is angry. He maintains this constantly.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator teaches the child by example that tranquillity is a good, thereby establishing self-control at the moment of anger, by which the soul is led to forbearance.
Through leading the emotions: The educator meets the child’s anger with calm and forbearance, not agitation, thereby planting tranquillity within him and teaching him to govern his emotion.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By calming the child’s anger, the educator intends to cultivate in him the forbearance that Allaah loves, not merely to silence him.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the forbearance that Allaah loves and makes hateful to him blameworthy anger, so that he grows up loving what Allaah loves.
Through patience (sabr): The educator bears the child’s fits of anger with forbearance and does not meet them with anger, thereby teaching him patience and training himself in it.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator meets the child’s anger with forbearance rather than anger, as an example, so he counsels him by his own state and teaches him patience through his deed.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator forestalls the fits of anger by ordering the child’s times of sleep and food, so that they diminish through the regulation of his rhythm.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator gradually teaches the child that anger is from Satan, thus habituating him to seek refuge and to be still when angry, so that he overcomes his enemy.
7. Attachment to a fixed routine.
The method of governance: Fixed remembrances (adhkaar) are placed in his routine at their proper occasions (at sleeping and eating), so that his innate disposition (fitrah) becomes accustomed to regular worship.
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator establishes the constancy of worship in the child’s routine and places fixed remembrances within it. He repeats them at their occasions.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator couples the faith-based routine with serenity and love, so that the child becomes fond of it. He intends to endear regular worship to him.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child the remembrance of each fixed time, such as sleeping and eating. He repeats it daily.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator keeps the child constant in fixed devotional acts within his routine. He persists in this.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator places fixed remembrances and acts of worship in the child’s routine, thereby establishing that the order of his life is a means by which he is led to Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator couples the faith-based routine with serenity and love, so the child grows fond of it with a feeling of intimacy.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By entrenching the faith-based routine, the educator intends to habituate the child to worship of Allaah, not merely to mechanical habit.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator endears to the child the constancy of the times of goodness, such as the times of remembrance, so that he grows up loving the perseverance that Allaah loves.
Through patience (sabr): The educator persists in the child’s faith-based routine with patience and steadfastness, so that the love of regular observance takes root in his innate disposition.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator persists in the faith-based routine as a steadfast example, so he counsels him by his own state, endearing regular observance to him.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator fixes the times of the faith-based routine with remembrance and supplication, so that the love of regular observance takes root through their regularity.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator places the remembrances of protection in the child’s routine, thereby fortifying him against Satan throughout the constancy of his day.
8. The beginning of self-awareness.
The method of governance: He is gently reminded that Allaah created him, fashioned him, and made his form excellent, so that his self-awareness develops coupled with gratitude to his Creator.
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator gently reminds the child that Allaah created him and fashioned him, so that his self-awareness develops coupled with his Creator. He repeats this.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child that Allaah created him and loves him, so he feels reassured. He intends to bind his sense of self to the love of Allaah.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child, gently, “Allaah created me.” He repeats this.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator shows the child the blessings of his body, giving thanks to Allaah for them. He maintains this constantly.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator gently reminds the child that Allaah created him, thereby establishing a self-awareness coupled with his Creator, by which his soul is led to Him.
Through leading the emotions: The educator plants in the child that Allaah created him and loves him, so he feels reassured, and his sense of self develops upon the love of Allaah.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): In acquainting the child with himself, the educator intends to bind him to his Creator, not to aggrandize his ego, so that he grows up humble before Allaah.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator binds the child’s self-awareness to the love of Allaah who created and fashioned him, so that he grows up loving his Creator and Benefactor.
Through patience (sabr): The educator reminds the child of the blessings of his creation with repetition and patience until his awareness that he is a servant of Allaah takes root.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator reminds the child of the blessings of his creation as a grateful example, so he counsels him by his own state, that he may be aware he is a servant of Allaah.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator seizes the child’s moments of clarity for repeated reminding, so that his awareness of servitude takes root through perseverance.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator founds the child’s self-awareness upon servitude to Allaah, so that he does not grow up conceited with a self-admiration that Satan and caprice would exploit.
9. Gradual control of excretion and the beginning of purity (tahaarah).
The method of governance: He is trained in cleanliness gently and patiently, and it is coupled with the beloved state of purity, so that his innate disposition becomes accustomed to the bodily cleanliness that Allaah loves.
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator establishes that Allaah loves purity, so he trains the child in cleanliness gently. He repeats this with patience.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator couples purity with love and encouragement, so that his innate disposition becomes fond of it. He intends to endear the cleanliness that Allaah loves.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child a simplified remembrance at the time of purification and praises him. He repeats this.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator trains the child in cleanliness gently and patiently, with praise. He maintains this constantly.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator trains the child in cleanliness, thereby establishing that Allaah loves purity, so that his soul is led by it to what pleases Him.
Through leading the emotions: The educator couples purity with encouragement and love, so that the child’s emotion grows fond of it and does not shun it.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By habituating the child to purity, the educator intends to prepare him for pure worship of Allaah, not merely outward cleanliness.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator endears to the child the purity that Allaah loves, so that he grows up loving the cleanliness that Allaah loves.
Through patience (sabr): The educator patiently trains the child in purity without harshness or haste, seeking reward, so that the child masters it gradually.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child in purity gently, not harshly, as an example, so he counsels him by his own state with deliberateness and the seeking of reward.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator organizes the times of purity training gradually, so that the child masters it in an ordered time without haste.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator habituates the child to purity and to cleansing after relieving oneself (istindjaa’), thereby fortifying him against the filth and laziness in which Satan delights.
10. Relatively independent eating.
The method of governance: He is habituated to pronouncing the name of Allaah (tasmiyah) before eating and to praising Him afterward, even if by gesture, so that his eating develops coupled with the remembrance of Allaah.
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator establishes that provision is from Allaah, so he habituates the child to pronouncing His name before eating. He repeats this.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator rejoices at the child’s independence in eating, with a love coupled with gratitude. He intends to bind his eating to the remembrance of Allaah.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child the pronouncing of Allaah’s name before eating and the praising of Him afterward. He repeats this.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator habituates the child to pronouncing Allaah’s name by gesture or utterance when he eats. He maintains this constantly.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator habituates the child to pronouncing Allaah’s name and praising Him at meals, thereby establishing that provision is from Allaah, so that his soul is led to giving thanks to Him.
Through leading the emotions: The educator rejoices at the child’s independence in eating, with a love coupled with gratitude, so that his emotion is bound to the praise of the Provider (al-Razzaaq).
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By habituating the child to the etiquette of eating, the educator intends to cultivate in him gratitude to Allaah, not mere independence.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator habituates the child to eating the good and lawful (tayyib halaal) and keeps him away from the foul, so that he becomes fond of what Allaah loves and abandons what He detests.
Through patience (sabr): The educator patiently bears the child’s learning to eat on his own and guides him gently, neither being harsh nor hasty.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator guides the child in eating on his own gently, as an example, so he counsels him by his own state with patience and regard for his stage of development.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator organizes the child’s mealtimes and trains him in independence during them, so that he learns in an ordered time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator habituates the child to pronouncing Allaah’s name over food and to eating with the right hand, thereby opposing Satan, who eats with his left.
11. Initial social interaction with peers.
The method of governance: He is gently encouraged to give to others and to share with them, and is praised for it, so that the seed of altruism (iethaar) sprouts in his innate disposition.
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator establishes that Allaah loves sharing, so he encourages the child to give. He repeats this gently.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator rejoices at the child’s sharing with love and praises him. He intends to plant the seed of altruism.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator says to the child, “Allaah loves those who share,” and praises him. He repeats this.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator encourages the child to give to others and to share with them. He maintains this constantly.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator encourages the child to share and to give, thereby establishing that giving is a good by which the soul is led to what Allaah loves.
Through leading the emotions: The educator rejoices at the child’s sharing with love and praises him, thereby planting the emotion of a seed of altruism and love for people for the sake of Allaah.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By habituating the child to sharing, the educator intends to cultivate in him giving for the sake of Allaah, not for showing off before people.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator endears to the child sharing with the people of faith and being good to them, so that he grows up upon love for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience during sharing, such as awaiting his turn, thereby habituating him to govern himself gently.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child in awaiting his turn in sharing, as an example, so he counsels him by his own state to govern himself and to have regard for others.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator habituates the child to awaiting his turn for a short while, thereby training him in the disciplining of time and in patience therein.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator habituates the child to giving and altruism, thereby striving against the soul’s miserliness that Satan and caprice exploit.
12. Kinetic curiosity and exploration.
The method of governance: His curiosity is directed toward the signs of Allaah in His creation (water, plants, animals) together with pronouncing His name, so that his exploration is bound to the veneration of the Creator.
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator directs the child’s curiosity toward the signs of Allaah in His creation and names them for him. He makes his exploration coupled with the Creator.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator rejoices at the child’s curiosity and binds it to the veneration of the Creator. He intends to plant a veneration of Allaah.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child “Subhaana Allaah” (Glory be to Allaah) upon exploring the wonders of creation. He repeats this.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator allows the child to explore what is good and safe, such as water and plants. He maintains this constantly.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator directs the child’s curiosity toward the signs of Allaah in His creation and names them, thereby establishing that his exploration is a means by which he is led to the veneration of the Creator.
Through leading the emotions: The educator binds the child’s wonder during exploration to the veneration of his Creator, so that his emotion develops upon reverence and not mere fascination.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By directing the child’s curiosity, the educator intends to acquaint him with his Lord so that he may worship Him, not to show off his cleverness.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator directs the child’s curiosity toward exploring the beneficial creation that Allaah loves and turns him away from what harms, so that he becomes fond of goodness.
Through patience (sabr): The educator patiently bears the child’s abundant exploration and his first questions, and guides them gently without exasperation.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator receives the child’s exploration and questions gently, as an example, so he counsels him by his own state to satisfy his curiosity with what is beneficial.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator seizes the moments of the child’s curiosity to direct him toward what is beneficial, thereby investing his mental activity in its proper time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator safeguards the child’s exploration from perils and harms, leaving no door open to the enemy through his curiosity, and directs him toward what is beneficial.
The age group from two to four years
The application of the disciplining of time in this age group across the four tracks (the educator embodies it and governs it):
Through purging/refinement (tasfiyah): It is built into the educator’s awareness that disciplining the child’s time begins with a fixed routine (sleep, wakefulness, food, and play at regular times), so that the child grows up upon order before he comprehends its meaning.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Serenity is planted in the child through the regularity of his day, and ordered time is bound to comfort and contentment, so that his soul grows fond of order rather than chaos.
Through the training of the tongue: He is taught the words of the times (“time for sleep,” “time for food,” “Bismillaah” at the beginning), so that he binds the utterance to the ordered act.
Through the training of the limbs: He is habituated to fixed appointments for sleep, food, and play, and is kept away from staying up late and excessive screens, so that his limbs are shaped upon an ordered rhythm that makes later commitment easier for him.
The application of the character trait of sincere counsel in this age group across the four tracks (the educator embodies it and governs it):
Through purging/refinement (tasfiyah): The educator’s conception is built upon the fact that the child is at the age of imitation, not of legal accountability (taklief), so his behavior is corrected by example and by a brief word rather than by rebuke; whatever is to be prevented is replaced for him with something good and he is gently turned away from it.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): His love for the one who guides him is planted by binding guidance to tenderness, praise, and a smile, so that rightness becomes associated in his mind with love and contentment rather than fear and stern rebuke.
Through the training of the tongue: He is taught the good word (“Say: Bismillaah,” “Say: al-Hamdu lillaah”), and is praised when he does well, while stern rebuke, coarse words, and shouting are avoided with him.
Through the training of the limbs: The right action is presented to him in deed, and he is taken gently by the hand toward it, and his error is corrected by an alternative rather than by punishment, in emulation of the gentleness of the Prophet ﷺ with little ones and the excellence of his kindness toward them.
The most beautiful names of Allaah and their pedagogical application in this age group
Building upon the names of the previous age group (al-Rahmaan, al-Rahiem, al-Razzaaq, al-Khaaliq) that the educator embodied for the infant, they are here deepened in a manner suited to the discerning, speaking child: after he used to receive them through the senses, he is now taught to pronounce them and to grasp the first of their meanings — so it is said to him, “Allaah created you, Allaah provides for you, Allaah is Merciful to you” — and the educator’s role shifts from mere embodiment to instilling and teaching. Then to that are added the names denoting the perception of Allaah’s watchfulness, upon which the pivot of vigilant awareness (muraaqabah) rests.
The name of Allaah: al-Samie3 (the All-Hearing)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
The signification of correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Samie3” signifies, by correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described as possessing perfect hearing by which He perceives all that is heard — its secret and its open, its hidden and its manifest — no hearing distracting Him from another.
The signification of implication (tadammun): It comprises the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of hearing subsisting in it.
The signification of entailment (iltizaam): It entails life and knowledge (for the one who hears is living and knowing), and it entails His encompassing of all the speech of His creation, and that He answers the supplicant and hears the one who complains. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allaah is Hearing and Seeing﴾ [al-Hadjdj 22:75], and He said: ﴿And Allaah hears your dialogue﴾ [al-Mudjaadilah 58:1].
The scholarly and exhortatory explanation: There is no whisper nor private converse but that Allaah hears it; He hears the crawling of the ant upon the rock in the darkness of night, and He hears the supplication of those who call upon Him, with the diversity of their tongues and needs, at one and the same time, without any confusion to Him. So whoever keeps present in his mind that Allaah is All-Hearing guards his tongue and makes his supplication sincere.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that Allaah hears your supplication, so supplicate Him often and be assured that He hears you. Warning: that He hears your backbiting, your lying, and your false speech, so guard your tongue, for the All-Hearing records your words against you.
The pedagogical application across the four tracks in this age group:
Through purging/refinement (tasfiyah): The child is taught that Allaah hears all that he says, so it is established in his mind that his speech is heard and observed by Allaah, nothing of it being hidden from Him.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): There is planted in him an awe that Allaah hears him and a love that Allaah is near and hears his supplication, so that his emotion develops upon both the vigilant awareness of the All-Hearing and hope in Him together.
Through the training of the tongue: He is habituated to say what is good and to supplicate Allaah with his small needs by his own tongue, and lying and abuse are avoided with him, so that his tongue develops upon what the All-Hearing loves to hear.
Through the training of the limbs: He is brought up to lower his voice from idle talk and to raise it with good, such as pronouncing Allaah’s name, remembrance, and the greeting of peace, so that his limbs — foremost among them his tongue — act in accordance with his knowledge that the All-Hearing is present.
The name of Allaah: al-Basier (the All-Seeing)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
The signification of correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Basier” signifies, by correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described as possessing perfect sight by which He perceives all that is seen — its minute and its great, in darkness and in light — no veil concealing it from Him.
The signification of implication (tadammun): It comprises the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of sight subsisting in it.
The signification of entailment (iltizaam): It entails life and knowledge, and it entails His encompassing of the sight of all the deeds of His creation, so that no deed, in secret or open, is absent from Him. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of all things﴾ [al-Mulk 67:19], and He said: ﴿Who sees you when you arise﴾ [al-Shu3araa’ 26:218].
The scholarly and exhortatory explanation: Allaah sees the footstep’s tread, and He sees the one who acts in his seclusion just as He sees him in his openness; and this name is the foundation of vigilant awareness (muraaqabah), which is the pinnacle of excellence (ihsaan): “that you worship Allaah as though you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He surely sees you” (Agreed upon (al-Bukhaarie and Muslim)). So whoever believes that Allaah sees him is ashamed that He should see him committing disobedience.
Encouragement and warning: Encouragement: that Allaah sees your good deeds and your obedience, even in secret, so that no deed is lost with Him. Warning: that He sees you when you disobey Him even if no one else sees you, so how can you hide from the One from whom nothing is hidden?
The pedagogical application across the four tracks in this age group:
Through purging/refinement (tasfiyah): It is planted in the child that Allaah sees him always, in the home and outside it, in light and in darkness, so that the first stage of vigilant awareness is established: that he is never alone.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): There is planted in him a modesty (hayaa’) before Allaah’s gaze upon him and a love that Allaah sees his good deeds, so that his emotion develops upon excellence in seclusion as in openness.
Through the training of the tongue: He is taught to say, when he is inclined toward something ugly, “Allaah sees me,” so that his tongue develops as a reminder to him of vigilant awareness.
Through the training of the limbs: He is trained to abandon what is ugly in his seclusion (such as taking what is not his) because Allaah sees him, even if his parents are absent from him, so that his limbs act in accordance with his knowledge that the All-Seeing is watching.
The name of Allaah: al-3Aliem (the All-Knowing)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
The signification of correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-3Aliem” signifies, by correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described as possessing perfect knowledge encompassing all things — their outward and their inward, their past, present, and future — not the weight of an atom escaping Him.
The signification of implication (tadammun): It comprises the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of encompassing knowledge subsisting in it.
The signification of entailment (iltizaam): It entails life, and it entails His encompassing of what is in the breasts and the innermost thoughts, and the perfection of His wisdom (for His knowledge requires the placing of things in their proper places). Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allaah is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Nisaa’ 4:176], and He said: ﴿He knows that which deceives the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghaafir 40:19].
The scholarly and exhortatory explanation: Allaah knows what you conceal and what you reveal, and He knows the stray notions of your heart before you utter them; He knows what has been, what will be, and what has not been — how it would be were it to be. So when the servant knows that his Lord is aware of his heart, he watches over his heart as he watches over his limbs.
Encouragement and warning: Encouragement: that Allaah knows the sincerity of your intention even if it is hidden from people, so He will reward you for it. Warning: that He knows the concealed evil within you, your ostentation, and your envy, so hiding them from creation avails you nothing while they are laid bare to the Creator.
The pedagogical application across the four tracks in this age group:
Through purging/refinement (tasfiyah): The child is taught that Allaah knows all things, even what is in the heart, so that it is established in his mind that hiding something from people hides nothing from Allaah.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): There is planted in him a vigilant awareness of the heart and not the limbs alone, and a love that Allaah should know good from him, so that his emotion develops upon the rectification of the inward.
Through the training of the tongue: He is habituated to truthfulness because Allaah knows the reality of the matter, so lying avails nothing, and thus his tongue develops upon truthfulness with the All-Knowing.
Through the training of the limbs: He is trained to sincerity in deeds, even a small one (such as a hidden charity), because the All-Knowing knows it and rewards it, so that his limbs act for the One who knows the secret and the open.
The name of Allaah: al-Malik (the Sovereign King)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
The signification of correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Malik” signifies, by correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described as possessing perfect sovereignty and disposal; for He is the Owner of all things, disposing of them by His command, to whom belong creation, command, and judgment.
The signification of implication (tadammun): It comprises the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of sovereignty and disposal.
The signification of entailment (iltizaam): It entails power, might, knowledge, wisdom, and self-sufficiency, and it entails the neediness of all besides Him toward Him and their submission to His sovereignty. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Sovereign of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Faatihah 1:4], and He said: ﴿To whom belongs [all] sovereignty this Day? To Allaah, the One, the Prevailing﴾ [Ghaafir 40:16].
The scholarly and exhortatory explanation: All kings are beneath His sovereignty, and all creatures are the bondservants of His dominion; none escapes His authority. He is the Sovereign of the Day of Recompense, on which false kingdoms are laid bare and His sovereignty alone remains. So whoever knows that Allaah is the Sovereign King humbles himself before Him and submits to His command.
Encouragement and warning: Encouragement: that the True Sovereign is generous, giving His servants from His treasuries that never run dry, so take refuge in Him. Warning: that He is the Sovereign of the Day of Recompense on which He calls His servants to account, so there is no fleeing from His sovereignty and no escape from His reckoning.
The pedagogical application across the four tracks in this age group:
Through purging/refinement (tasfiyah): The child is taught that Allaah is the Owner of all things: the heaven, the earth, and what is in them, and that all that he has is from the giving of the Sovereign King, so that it is established that all sovereignty belongs to Allaah.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): There is planted in him the greatness of the Sovereign King, the humility of servitude to Him, and love of Him, so that his emotion develops upon submission to His command rather than to the command of any other when it contradicts His.
Through the training of the tongue: He is taught “al-Hamdu lillaah” and “Maa shaa’a Allaah” upon seeing blessings, as an acknowledgment that they are the possession of Allaah, so that his tongue develops upon ascribing sovereignty to Allaah.
Through the training of the limbs: He is habituated to seek permission for what is not his and to return what he has taken without right, as an upbringing upon the principle that sovereignty belongs to Allaah and to whomever Allaah has granted ownership, so that his limbs act in accordance with the veneration of the Owner.
The detailed innate characteristics specific to this age stage, and how to govern them pedagogically toward the veneration of Allaah and the governance and direction of the deeds of the hearts
This is a clarification for the educator on how to benefit from this section: every innate trait is an energy that Allaah has deposited in the young one, neither to be suppressed nor neglected, but rather to be directed toward the veneration of Allaah and His worship. The method of treatment here is: the trait and its description are mentioned, then its general facilitation, then it is treated across the four tracks: purging/refinement (tasfiyah) (for the mind), purification of the soul (tazkiyah) (for the heart), the training of the tongue, and the training of the limbs.
Every trait is treated in each track by four rabbaanie methods derived from the Book and the Sunnah, and beneath each method are six practical means. Let the educator know that the detailed elaboration is given only in the first means of each method — through an exposition of the educator’s action, his follow-up with the one being raised, then his response when he sees good and when he sees otherwise, in the child’s thinking, feeling, speech, and interaction through his limbs — then the remaining five means are mentioned briefly, and their treatment proceeds upon the very approach of the first means, so the educator measures them against it.
The educator observes in this that the reward of the one being raised should be bound to Allaah — through His love, good deeds, and merit points — not to a gift from himself; and that he should keep present sincerity and the seeking of reward, and that guidance is in the hand of Allaah alone, so he praises Him if he sees good and is patient and supplicates for guidance if he sees otherwise. The pivot of this stage is upon innate instilling and gentle reminding, together with sincerity of intention and supplication.
Children at this age stage possess a number of innate characteristics, among them:
Excessive curiosity: the repetition of questions: “Why? How?”
His curiosity can be invested to bind him to Allaah: “Because Allaah is the One who created everything,” “Allaah loves us and so He gave us water.”
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
With every question of “why” or “how,” the educator concludes his answer with “because Allaah created it thus by His wisdom.” He repeats this with every question daily until the child ascribes everything to Allaah.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator binds the child’s answers to the love of Allaah: “Allaah gave you this because He loves you.” He shows his own delight so that the love of Allaah becomes ingrained in the child’s heart with every discovery.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child a brief answer: “Allaah is the Creator.” He asks him to repeat it joyfully every day in endearing situations.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator takes the child by the hand to show him in reality what he asks about (a tree, the sky, water). He raises his own hands in praise of Allaah before him so that he may learn gratitude through the limbs.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator directs the child’s curiosity from random questioning to what is beneficial, habituating him to the fact that asking about Allaah and His creation is the first seeking of knowledge by which his soul is led to the truth.
Through leading the emotions: The educator restrains the child’s eagerness so that he does not interrupt, and transforms his wonder upon the answer into the veneration of the Creator and awe of Him.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator habituates the child to ask in order to know the truth, not to draw attention, thereby planting that seeking knowledge is an act of worship of Allaah.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator directs the child’s questions toward what Allaah loves and what benefits, and turns him away from what does not concern him, so that he loves beneficial knowledge.
Through patience (sabr): The educator answers the child’s repeated questions with patience and without exasperation, teaching him patience in seeking the answer.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator answers the child’s questions gently, as an example, so he counsels him by his own state to satisfy his curiosity with the truth and habituates him to asking well.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator seizes the moments of the child’s curiosity to answer him, thereby investing his eagerness to learn in its appropriate time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator takes heed that Satan may draw the child’s curiosity toward asking about what does not benefit, so he turns him toward what is beneficial.
Expansion of vocabulary: simple sentences, then more complex ones.
Repeated faith-based words are woven into his speech, such as: “Bismillaah,” “al-Hamdu lillaah,” “Allaah is Generous,” so that they become part of his lexicon.
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator explains the simplified meaning of “Bismillaah”: “we begin with Allaah before everything.” He repeats it with every daily activity the child does.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator sows the love of the faith-based words in the child’s heart by showing his joy upon hearing them from him. He praises him for them, so that the love of them becomes ingrained in his heart.
Third: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
The educator instills in the child daily: “Bismillaah, al-Hamdu lillaah, Subhaana Allaah.” He asks him to repeat them before eating and after it and in tangible situations.
Fourth: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator joins to the remembrance a light, tangible movement (extending the palm, a gesture with the hand). He repeats the action along with the utterance until it is imprinted upon the child’s innate disposition.
Governance through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator weaves the words of remembrance into the child’s vocabulary, thereby establishing a tongue that pronounces that by which the soul is led to Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator shows his joy when the child pronounces a faith-based word, so that the emotion of his language is bound to an intimacy with remembrance.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator habituates the child to saying the remembrance seeking the Face of Allaah, not to boasting of his many words.
Through love, fear, loyalty, and disavowal: The educator endears to the child good speech and keeps him away from ugly utterance, so that his tongue develops upon what Allaah loves.
Through patience (sabr): The educator repeats the instilling of the faith-based words in the child with patience until they take root in his tongue.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator instills the faith-based words in the child as a loving example, so he counsels him by his own state to fill his tongue with the remembrance of Allaah.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator designates regular times for instilling, so that the faith-based utterance takes root in his tongue through perseverance.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator safeguards the child’s language from the ugly words that Satan finds pleasing, thereby fortifying his tongue.
Love of social imitation: playing the role of the father, mother, or teacher.
He is encouraged to imitate the elders in prayer or in saying the remembrances, and it is said to him: “You are like daddy when he says Bismillaah.”
First: Addressing it through purging/refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that imitating the righteous pleases Allaah. He mentions to him the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions as an example with every situation.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants love of the Prophet ﷺ in the child’s heart by displaying his own love for him. He praises the child whenever he imitates him, so that his love may be confirmed.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks the child to say what adults say in worship (“Bismillaah,” “Allaahu akbar”). He repeats this with him at every devotional occasion.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator prays in front of the child and lets him imitate him. He takes him by the hand so that he performs the movements together with him, with joy and tenderness.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator directs the child’s imitation toward emulating one who leads his own soul through obedience to Allaah, thereby establishing a following (iqtidaa’) by which his soul is led to good.
Through leading the emotions: The educator rejoices at the child’s imitation of good, so that the emotion of his emulation becomes tied to the atmosphere of obedience.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to imitate good for Allaah’s sake and not to be praised, thereby implanting sincerity in his emulation.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the imitation of the righteous in prayer and remembrance, and keeps him away from imitating the people of evil, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator persists in being a good role model with patience until the child’s imitation of good becomes firmly rooted.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator persists in good example, thereby advising the child by his conduct before his speech, so that his imitation of good becomes firmly rooted.
Through disciplining time: The educator maintains his example at all times, so that the child’s emulation becomes firmly rooted through constancy rather than interruption.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator is wary lest the child imitate an evil that Satan beautifies in his surroundings, thereby safeguarding his example.
Imaginative play: stories and roles from his imagination.
Stories are told to him about a child who loves Allaah, helps people, and always says “al-hamdu lillaah,” so as to integrate faith into his imagination.
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator tells the child short stories about a child who loves Allaah and obeys. He explains them to him with examples from his daily life.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child’s imagination the wish to be a “hero” who loves Allaah and helps others. He praises him when he does this in his play.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks that the characters of his play say “Bismillaah” and “al-hamdu lillaah.” He joins him in play, repeating this with him.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator acts out with the child roles of kindness (ihsaan): feeding a doll, helping a friend. He multiplies such scenes in his play.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator directs the child’s imagination toward stories of good and their emulation, thereby establishing an imagination by which the soul is led to the love of Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator implants in the child’s imaginative play feelings of love for good, so that his emotion is nurtured upon what is wholesome.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By directing the child’s imagination, the educator intends to raise him upon love of good for Allaah’s sake, not mere amusement.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the roles of good — like a child who loves Allaah and helps people — and keeps him away from enacting evil, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator shares in the child’s purposeful play with patience and constancy, so that his inclination toward good becomes settled.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator shares in the child’s purposeful play and guides him within it as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to choose the most beneficial play and to incline toward good.
Through disciplining time: The educator sets a regular time for purposeful play in the child’s day, so that he grows accustomed to playing at its proper time and his inclination toward good becomes settled.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator safeguards the child’s imagination against imitating the violence and evil that Satan beautifies.
Love of physical exploration: running, climbing, jumping.
In his exploration he is connected to the Creator: “Did you see the sky? Allaah is the One who created it!” “Allaah gave you a strong body to run with.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator comments on every movement of the child by ascribing it to Allaah: “Allaah gave you a strong body.” He repeats it until it is implanted in his conception.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants love of Allaah’s blessings in the child’s heart by giving thanks for them with him. He rejoices before him when he runs and praises Allaah together with him.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks for the saying of “al-hamdu lillaah” after every physical activity. He repeats this with him each time with joy.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator channels the child’s physical energy into beneficial tasks (fetching something, tidying a toy). He repeats them with joy and praise.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator connects the child’s physical exploration to the Creator, thereby establishing that his activity leads him to the veneration of Allaah and to giving thanks to Him.
Through leading the emotions: The educator connects the child’s wonder at what he explores to the veneration of his Creator, so that his emotion is nurtured upon reverence and not mere fascination.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): By directing the child’s activity, the educator intends to acquaint him with his Lord so that he may worship Him, not merely for fun.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator directs the child’s exploration toward that of His creation which Allaah loves, and restrains him from what is harmful, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator patiently bears the child’s abundant movement and exploration, and guides it with forbearance and without suppression.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator guides the child’s movement and exploration with forbearance and not suppression, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to channel his energy into what is beneficial.
Through disciplining time: The educator provides the child with organized times for exploration, so that he expends his energy at a fruitful time and not in chaos.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator safeguards the child’s exploration from perils, leaving no door open to the enemy in his movement.
Grasping the principle of “mine” and “yours”: a clear sense of ownership.
This understanding is used to teach that “Allaah is the One who gave us everything, even your toy, which is why we thank Him.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that everything in truth belongs to Allaah, who gave it to him to use. He repeats it with tangible daily examples.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants love of sharing in the child’s heart. He praises him when he gives others some of his toys and rejoices before him.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks the child to say “Allaah gave me this” at his blessings. He repeats it with him at every daily occasion.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator teaches the child to share his toys and food. He begins with small, manageable situations, with joy and praise.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator teaches the child that Allaah is the Owner, the Giver, thereby establishing that all ownership comes from Him, so that his soul is led to give thanks to Him.
Through leading the emotions: The educator disciplines the child’s sense of ownership so that it does not become excessive, and implants in him contentment and satisfaction with what Allaah has apportioned.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to give and share for Allaah’s sake and not to be praised, thereby implanting sincerity in his giving.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the giving and sharing that Allaah loves, and makes miserliness hateful to him, so that he grows familiar with what Allaah loves.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience if another takes something, and accustoms him to master himself gently.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator trains the child in patience if another takes something, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to master himself and to observe the right of others.
Through disciplining time: The educator accustoms the child to await his turn for a short while, thereby training him to master his desire in its proper time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator accustoms the child to giving, thereby struggling against the miserliness of the soul that Satan and caprice exploit.
Developing memory: recalling events of previous days.
The formulas of remembrance (adhkaar) are repeated with him daily, and he is reminded: “Do you remember, yesterday we said Bismillaah before eating? Allaah was pleased with you.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that remembering Allaah is a blessing that He loves. He ties his memory to the daily adhkaar at every occasion.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child’s heart love of remembering Allaah. He rejoices before him when he recalls a dhikr he learned yesterday.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator reminds the child daily of the adhkaar he has learned. He asks him to recall them with joy and praise.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator repeats with the child the adhkaar of occasions (food, sleep) each day at the same time, until they cling to his memory.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator repeats the adhkaar with the child so that he memorizes them, thereby establishing a memory in which meanings are stored by which the soul is led to Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator connects the good that the child remembers with joy and love, so that his memory becomes tied to the atmosphere of faith.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to memorize the dhikr for Allaah’s sake and not for show, thereby implanting sincerity in his acquisition of it.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator has the child memorize the dhikr and Qur’an that Allaah loves, and keeps him away from memorizing idle talk, so that his memory grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator repeats the memorization with patience and constancy until it becomes firmly rooted in the child’s memory.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator has the child memorize what is wholesome, as a loving role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to fill his memory with the speech of Allaah.
Through disciplining time: The educator sets aside short, regular times for memorization, so that what is memorized becomes firmly rooted through constancy rather than exhaustion.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator fills the child’s memory with good, leaving in it no emptiness that Satan might fill with the memorizing of idle talk.
Displaying feelings of empathy and jealousy.
He is taught that Allaah loves those who show empathy: “Allaah loves the one who is glad when he sees his brother happy.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah loves the one who empathizes with others. He mentions tangible examples to him at moments of empathy.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child’s heart love of making others happy for Allaah’s sake. He rejoices before him when he shows empathy toward his brothers.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks for the saying of “Allaah loves you” to his brother or friend. He repeats it with him at every affectionate occasion.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator channels the child’s empathy into tangible actions (an embrace, help). He praises him when he does them.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator directs the child’s empathy toward what Allaah loves, and disciplines his jealousy, thereby establishing feelings by which the soul is led to good.
Through leading the emotions: The educator teaches the child to discipline his jealousy so that it does not turn into envy, and implants in him joy at the good that comes to his brothers.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to empathy and kindness for Allaah’s sake and not to be seen as empathetic, thereby implanting sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the love of good for his brothers, and makes envy hateful to him, so that he is nurtured upon love for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience and in restraining jealousy when another is favored, and accustoms him to contentment.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator addresses the child’s jealousy with justice and gentleness, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to be content and to love good for others.
Through disciplining time: The educator divides his time among his children with justice, thereby cutting off the causes of jealousy by treating them fairly in his times.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator alerts that envy is from Satan, thereby accustoming the child to rejoice for his brothers rather than to envy them.
An increasing ability to follow multi-step instructions.
This ability is employed in contexts of faith: “We put on our shoes, we say Bismillaah, and then we walk and supplicate.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that obedience to adults is part of obedience to Allaah. He invests his ability to follow instructions in teaching him this.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants love of obedience in the child’s heart by tying it to Allaah’s pleasure. He praises him when he obeys and rejoices before him.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks the child to say “I hear and obey” or “Right away” with joy. He repeats this with him with every instruction.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator gives the child multi-step instructions that he ties to Allaah (“We dress, we say Bismillaah, we walk”). He praises him for completing them.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator employs the child’s ability to follow steps in contexts of obedience, thereby establishing a submission by which the soul is led to the command of Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator connects the child’s compliance with joy and love, so that the emotion of his obedience becomes tied to an intimacy with good.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to comply with the command of good for Allaah’s sake, not merely to please him.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child compliance with what Allaah loves, and keeps him away from obeying one who commands evil, so that he is nurtured upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience until he completes the multi-step task, thereby accustoming him to perseverance.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to complete the task, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to persevere and not to flit from one thing to another.
Through disciplining time: The educator divides the task over a graduated period of time, thereby accustoming the child to complete his work in its proper time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator accustoms the child to comply with good, so that he does not grow up quick to obey every commander, even one commanding an evil that he beautifies.
Love of daily routine: a sense of security in repetition.
Remembrance (dhikr) is made part of the routine: “Every day we say al-hamdu lillaah after eating, right?”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that the constancy of the daily adhkaar increases Allaah’s love for him. He makes them part of his fixed routine.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child’s heart an intimacy with the repeated adhkaar. He rejoices before him at their recitation each day with joy.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator introduces a single dhikr at each fixed time (before eating, at sleep). He repeats it with him daily at the same time.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator keeps company with the child in a fixed routine that includes acts of worship (a symbolic ablution, facing the qiblah). He makes them familiar.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator places fixed adhkaar in the child’s routine, thereby establishing that the order of his day leads him to Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator pairs the faith-based routine with security and love, so that the child grows familiar with it through an emotion of intimacy.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to worship within his routine for Allaah’s sake, not as mere habit.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the constancy of the times of good, so that he is nurtured upon love of the perseverance that Allaah loves.
Through patience (sabr): The educator persists in the child’s faith-based routine with steadfastness and patience, so that love of constancy becomes firmly rooted.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator makes the child’s faith-based routine firm and adheres to it constantly, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct so as to make perseverance in good beloved to him.
Through disciplining time: The educator fixes the times of the faith-based routine, so that love of constancy becomes firmly rooted through their regularity.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator places in the child’s routine the adhkaar of protection, thereby fortifying him against Satan in the constancy of his day.
Constantly testing limits: to learn the reactions.
A method of tender, faith-based watchfulness is used: “Allaah sees us now, and He loves the one who heeds what he is told.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah sees and hears everything. He repeats it with tenderness so that the restraint of watchfulness (muraaqabah) may be implanted in him.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child’s heart a tender awe (khashyah) of Allaah: “Allaah loves the one who heeds what he is told.” He rejoices before him at his obedience.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator prompts the child with the remembrance “Allaah sees me” at various occasions. He repeats it with him gently at every transgression.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator sets clear, graduated limits, and rebukes him gently (with a stern rebuke, zajr) when he oversteps them, through an exhortation (wa3dh) he can grasp. He then restores his bond with him through tenderness afterward.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator sets for the child tender, firm limits, thereby establishing that Allaah has limits by which the soul is led so that it does not transgress them.
Through leading the emotions: The educator meets the child’s testing of limits with forbearance and steadiness rather than agitation, thereby implanting in him respect for the limit with serenity.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to observe the limit out of watchfulness of Allaah and not merely out of fear of him, thereby implanting watchfulness of Allaah.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator teaches the child that observing what Allaah loves is good and overstepping His limit is evil, so that he is nurtured upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator is patient with the child’s repeated testing of limits, and holds firm to the limit with forbearance and without harshness.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator holds firm to the limit with forbearance when the child tests it, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct through gentle firmness rather than harshness.
Through disciplining time: The educator chooses the times of the child’s calm to establish the limits, thereby containing his testing at a suitable time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator gradually teaches the child that overstepping the limit gladdens Satan, thereby making the observance of Allaah’s limits beloved to him.
Attempting to influence the decisions of adults.
This is invested by involving him in making a decision that pleases Allaah: “What do you think — shall we choose what makes my Lord happy?”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that the correct decision is the one that pleases Allaah. He invests his participation in the decision to teach him this.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child’s heart love of choosing what pleases Allaah. He rejoices before him when he chooses good.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks the child: “What is it that makes Allaah happy?” and he tries to answer. He prompts him joyfully if he does not know.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator involves the child in simple choices that please Allaah (giving a toy in charity, giving food). He praises him for his choice.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator involves the child in a decision that pleases Allaah, thereby establishing that his opinion is directed toward that by which the soul is led to good.
Through leading the emotions: The educator gently disciplines the child’s insistence, thereby teaching him to express his opinion with courtesy and serenity.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to propose good for Allaah’s sake and not to attain his own caprice, thereby implanting sincerity in his opinion.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator directs the child’s suggestions toward what Allaah loves, and turns them away from what He hates, so that he loves good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience and contentment if his opinion is not adopted, thereby accustoming him to master himself.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child contentment if his opinion is not adopted, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to master himself and to submit.
Through disciplining time: The educator gives the child time to express his opinion and then guides him, thereby accustoming him to patience in its proper time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator directs the child’s desire to influence toward good, so that it does not turn into an obstinacy that caprice and Satan beautify.
The ability to play with others: the beginning of developing social skills.
He is taught that “Allaah loves the one who shares his toy,” and the concept of social obedience through pleasing Allaah is instilled.
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah loves sharing. He mentions this to him at every occasion of play with others.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants love of altruism (iethaar) in the child’s heart. He praises him when he gives his turn to another and rejoices before him.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks the child to say “Here you are” and “Thank you” during play. He repeats them with him at every occasion.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator trains the child to give his turn to another. He makes this a habit in every game with peers.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator teaches the child the etiquette of playing with others, thereby establishing a manner of dealing by which the soul is led to the good character that Allaah loves.
Through leading the emotions: The educator teaches the child to discipline his feelings during play so that he neither becomes angry nor transgresses, and implants in him gentleness.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to kindness toward his companions for Allaah’s sake and not to be praised, thereby implanting sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the sharing with and love of the people of good, and keeps him away from evil companions, so that he is nurtured upon love for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience and in awaiting his turn during play, and accustoms him to master himself.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to await his turn during play, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to master himself and to be considerate of others.
Through disciplining time: The educator accustoms the child to await his turn for a short while, thereby training him to manage time in his play.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator safeguards the child from evil companions, who are among the soldiers of Satan, thereby establishing the companionship of good.
Expressing anger or sadness in a clearer way.
He is helped to manage his feelings: “Allaah loves the one who calms down and says al-hamdu lillaah, not the one who screams.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah loves calm and hates shouting. He repeats it gently at moments of anger.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants love of patience in the child’s heart. He praises him when he suppresses his anger and calms down, and rejoices before him.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator prompts the child, upon anger, to say “I seek refuge in Allaah from Satan.” He repeats it with him tenderly in the moment.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator teaches the child to sit down or to make a simple ablution upon anger. He makes it a clear action for release.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator teaches the child to calm himself upon anger and to say something good, thereby establishing the self-mastery by which it is led to forbearance.
Through leading the emotions: The educator teaches the child to express his anger and sadness in a controlled manner, and implants in him serenity.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to control his anger out of watchfulness of Allaah, thereby implanting sincerity in his forbearance.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the forbearance that Allaah loves, and makes blameworthy anger hateful to him, so that he is nurtured upon love of what Allaah loves.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience upon anger and sadness, and accustoms him to the istirdjaa3 (saying “innaa lillaahi wa-innaa ilayhi raadji3oen”) and to contentment.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator trains the child in patience upon anger and sadness, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to make the istirdjaa3 and to be content.
Through disciplining time: The educator gives the child time to calm down when he is agitated, thereby accustoming him to master himself in its very moment.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that anger is from Satan, thereby accustoming him to seek refuge and to grow still at its onset.
Love of taking part in simple household chores.
He is motivated by tying them to Allaah: “You are helping Mama? Allaah is pleased with you; He loves the one who helps his family.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah loves the one who assists his family. He invests his enthusiasm for participation in teaching him this.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants love of serving the family in the child’s heart. He rejoices before him when he helps and praises him.
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks the child to say “I want to help you, mother” before the task. He repeats it with him daily.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator gives the child small, manageable tasks daily (arranging the shoes, carrying something). He praises him and ties them to Allaah’s pleasure.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator connects the child’s participation in chores to the love of Allaah, thereby establishing that beneficial work leads him to the pleasure of Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator rejoices at the child’s help and praises him, thereby implanting an emotion of love for beneficial work.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to help for Allaah’s sake and to assist his family seeking reward, not merely to be praised.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator makes beloved to the child the assisting of his family and the kindness toward them that Allaah loves, so that he is nurtured upon dutifulness (birr).
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience and in completing the task, and accustoms him to perseverance.
Through sincere advice (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to complete his task, as a role model, thereby advising him by his conduct to persevere and not to abandon it.
Through disciplining time: The educator sets a time for the child to complete his task, thereby accustoming him to adhere to the time of his work.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator accustoms the child to be active in good, so that he does not leave his free time to the laziness that Satan loves.
Positive interaction when encouraged.
Praise is made saturated with faith: “Maa shaa’a Allaah! Allaah loves the children who say Bismillaah.”
First: Treating it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that the best praise is Allaah’s pleasure with him. He ties his praise to this at every occasion.
Second: Treating it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
The educator plants in the child’s heart love of attaining Allaah’s pleasure. He praises him upon doing good by saying: “Allaah is pleased with you.”
Third: Treating it through upbringing — training the tongue
The educator asks for the saying of “al-hamdu lillaah” upon hearing praise. He repeats it with him so that he grows accustomed to returning the credit to Allaah.
Fourth: Treating it through upbringing — training the limbs
The educator accompanies his praise of the child with a tender gesture (a pat, an embrace, a smile). He repeats it whenever he does good.
Direction through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the self and seeking knowledge: The educator praises the child by connecting him to Allaah, thereby establishing that all merit belongs to Allaah, so that his soul is led to His pleasure and not to the praise of people.
Through leading the emotions: The educator praises the child with balanced joy coupled with the pleasure of Allaah, thereby implanting an emotion of joy in obedience.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to work for the pleasure of Allaah and not for the praise of people, thereby implanting sincerity and guarding against ostentation (riyaa’).
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal: The educator ties his praise to Allaah’s love of the good deed, so that the child is nurtured upon love of what Allaah loves.
