Building upon the names of the two preceding groups (al-Rahmaan [the Most Merciful], al-Rahiem [the Bestower of Mercy], al-Razzaaq [the Ever-Providing], and al-Khaaliq [the Creator]; then al-Samie3 [the All-Hearing], al-Basier [the All-Seeing], al-3Aliem [the All-Knowing], and al-Malik [the Sovereign]), they are here deepened in a manner suited to the child of the age of questioning, of imagination, and of the first discernment between good and evil: his question about Allaah is answered in a manner suited to his intellect, what he sees of the magnificence of the universe is linked to the magnificence of its Creator, and he is reminded that the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the All-Knowing is fully informed of him. Then are added the names of magnificence, of generosity, and of forgiveness that build in his heart both reverence and hope together.
The Name of Allaah: al-3Adhiem (the Magnificent)
The Meaning and Its Three Indications:
The indication of correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-3Adhiem” indicates, by way of correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described with the perfection of magnificence in His Essence and His Attributes — a magnificence that minds cannot encompass and whose true reality understandings cannot grasp; for He is the Magnificent, before whom everything else is insignificant.
The indication of inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and of the attribute of absolute magnificence.
The indication of entailment (iltizaam): It entails all the remaining attributes of perfection (for His magnificence is in His knowledge, His power, His mercy, and His wisdom), and it entails the obligation of venerating Him, of exalting Him, and of the submission of hearts to Him; Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Magnificent﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255].
The scholarly and exhortative explanation: For the seven heavens and the earths are in His palm like a mustard seed in the hand of one of us, and He will fold up the heavens with His right hand on the Day of Resurrection. So when the heart of the servant is filled with the magnificence of Allaah, everything besides Him becomes small in his eye, so that he does not magnify his own disobedience and does not fear anyone [at the expense of] the truth. And this name is the spirit of this entire book: the veneration of Allaah.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that the magnificence of Allaah entails the magnificence of His giving and His reward, so whoever worships a Magnificent One attains a magnificent recompense. And warning: that His magnificence entails the magnificence of His seizing and His punishment, so making light of His command is making light of a Magnificent One, and His punishment is in proportion to His magnificence.
The Pedagogical Application through the Four Pathways in this Group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The mighty created things the child beholds (the sky, the mountains, the sea) are linked to the greatness of their Creator, so that it is established in his mind that the Creator of what is great is greater still, and that Allaah is greater than everything.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Reverence and awe of Allaah are instilled in his heart, so that his emotion is nurtured upon the veneration of Allaah, which is the foundation of all worship.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to say “Allaahu akbar (Allaah is greater)” and “Subhaana Rabbiya al-3Adhiem (Glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent),” and is habituated to repeat them with reflection, so that his tongue is nurtured upon the veneration of the Magnificent.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained in the postures of veneration in the prayer (the bowing and the prostration) and in the etiquette of the remembrance of Allaah, so that his limbs translate the reverence of the Magnificent.
The Name of Allaah: al-Kariem (the Most Generous)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Kariem” denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described with the perfection of generosity, munificence, and benevolence; He is the abundant in good, the One who gives without recompense and without being asked, who gives before He is asked and forgives after disobedience.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of generosity and munificence.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails absolute self-sufficiency (for the Generous is self-sufficient), and mercy, forbearance, and forgiveness, and it entails the vastness of His giving, so that His treasuries are never depleted. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous﴾ [al-Infitaar 82:6].
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: His generosity encompasses every existent thing; He gives to the believer and the disbeliever, to the obedient and the disobedient; He multiplies a single good deed tenfold, up to seven hundredfold, up to many times more; He conceals the ugly deed and pardons much. So whoever knows the generosity of his Lord feels ashamed to meet His generosity with disobedience.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that the generosity of Allaah has no limit, so hold a good opinion of Him and aspire to His bounty, His giving, and His forgiveness. Warning: that whoever meets the generosity of the Generous with disbelief and disobedience has been deceived by the world and deserves to be deprived on account of his evil conduct.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child is taught that every good thing he is given comes from the generosity of Allaah, so that gratitude to the Bestower of blessings and the attribution of all bounty to Him is established in his mind.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Love of Allaah the Generous, aspiration to His generosity, and shame at wronging Him are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon gratitude and hope.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to praise and give thanks when he receives a gift, and is habituated to supplication while calling to mind the generosity of the One being asked, so that his tongue is nurtured upon giving thanks to the Generous.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained in generosity, giving, and self-sacrifice in emulation of the generosity of Allaah—for whoever is treated generously acts generously—so that his limbs act in accordance with love of the Generous.
The Name of Allaah: al-Ghafoer (the Most Forgiving)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Ghafoer” denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described with abundant and vast forgiveness; forgiveness is the concealing of a sin together with the remission of its punishment—He is the One who forgives all sins for whoever repents.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of vast forgiveness.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails forbearance, mercy, generosity, and power (for the One who forgives is capable of punishment yet pardons it), and it entails the opening of the door of repentance. Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿But indeed, I am the Perpetual Forgiver of whoever repents and believes and does righteousness﴾ [Taahaa 20:82].
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: However great the servant’s sin may be, the forgiveness of Allaah is greater; He forgives the sin even were it to reach the horizon of the sky, if the servant seeks forgiveness and turns back to Him, and He rejoices at the repentance of His servant with the utmost joy. So let no sinner despair of His forgiveness, nor let anyone persisting [in sin] feel secure from His punishment.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that the door of forgiveness is open and is never closed, so hasten to repentance however much you have sinned, for Allaah forgives all sins. Warning: that forgiveness is for whoever repents and turns back, not for whoever persists and grows arrogant, so do not take the vastness of forgiveness as a pretext for persistence [in sin].
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child—now that he has begun to err—is taught that Allaah forgives whoever errs and then feels remorse and seeks forgiveness, so that it is established in his mind that a mistake is remedied by repentance, not by despair nor by persisting in it.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): The emotion of hope after a mistake, and the remorse that impels toward setting things right, are planted within him, so that his soul is nurtured between the fear of sin and the hope of forgiveness.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to say “Astaghfiru Allaah (I seek Allaah’s forgiveness)” and “Rabbi ighfir lie (My Lord, forgive me)” when he errs, so that his tongue is nurtured upon seeking forgiveness.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained—when he errs—to apologize, to turn back, and to repair what he has spoiled, as a translation of repentance into action, so that his limbs act in accordance with the hope [placed] in al-Ghafoer.
The Name of Allaah: al-Quddoes (the Most Holy)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Quddoes” denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah declared free of every deficiency and defect, hallowed above all that does not befit His majesty; He is the Pure, sanctified above resembling the creation and above every defect.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and its exaltation above all deficiencies.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails the perfection of all His attributes (for declaring Him free [of deficiencies] entails affirming their opposites from among the [attributes of] perfection), and the obligation of venerating and hallowing Him.
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿He is Allaah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection﴾ [al-Hashr 59:23], and He said: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is exalting Allaah, the Sovereign, the Pure﴾ [al-Djumu3ah 62:1]. The foundation for the knowledge of these names is the hadith of Aboe Hurayrah: “Indeed, Allaah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise” (Narrated by al-Bukhaarie, no. 2736, and Muslim, no. 2677).
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: For Allaah is hallowed and sanctified above every deficiency that the ignorant ascribe to Him: above a consort and a child, above a partner and a peer, and above incapacity, sleep, and fatigue. So when the servant hallows his Lord, he declares Him free in his heart of every defect, and purifies his heart, his tongue, and his deeds so as to befit the servitude owed to al-Quddoes.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that al-Quddoes loves purity and cleanness from all filth in His servants, so whoever purifies himself outwardly and inwardly, Allaah loves him. Warning: that ascribing deficiency to al-Quddoes, or defiling the heart with associationism (shirk) and acts of disobedience, contradicts His sanctification, and Allaah detests it.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child—at the age of first conceptualization—is taught that Allaah is perfect, with no defect in Him and no deficiency, and that there is nothing like unto Him, so that the exaltation of Allaah above resembling the creation is established in his mind.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): The awe of hallowing Allaah and love of His purity are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon venerating al-Quddoes and declaring Him free [of all defect].
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to say “Subhaana Allaah (Glory be to Allaah)” and “Subhaana Rabbiya al-A3laa (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High)” as a declaration of Allaah’s transcendence, so that his tongue is nurtured upon hallowing Allaah.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is habituated to physical purity (ablution and cleanliness), and this is linked to the purity of the heart, so that his limbs translate the hallowing of al-Quddoes.
The Name of Allaah: al-Salaam (the Source of Peace)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Salaam” denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah that is free of every deficiency, defect, and blemish; He is the One from whom [all] soundness comes, from whom security and peace in this world and the Hereafter are sought, and who greets His allies with peace in Paradise.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and its soundness from every deficiency, and His being the source of [all] soundness.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails the perfection of His life, His knowledge, and His power (since soundness from deficiency entails the perfection of its opposite), and that all soundness is from Him.
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Bestower of Faith, the Overseer﴾ [al-Hashr 59:23], and He said, concerning His greeting of the people of Paradise: ﴿[And] “Peace,” a word from a Merciful Lord﴾ [Yaa Sien 36:58]. And when the Prophet ﷺ concluded his prayer with the closing salaam, he would say: “O Allaah, You are Peace and from You is peace. Blessed are You, O Owner of Majesty and Honor” (Narrated by Muslim, no. 591, from the hadith of Thawbaan).
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: For Allaah is al-Salaam, who is free of every defect, and from Him is sought soundness from the evils of this world and the Hereafter; so security and peace are sought from none but Him. Whoever knows that his Lord is al-Salaam takes refuge in Him, seeking the soundness of his religion, his heart, and his body.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that al-Salaam greets His allies with peace and settles them in the Abode of Peace (Daar al-Salaam), so seek your soundness from Him. Warning: that whoever turns away from Him will not attain soundness and will be encompassed by fears in this world and by torment in the Hereafter.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child is taught that it is Allaah who grants security and safety, and that all safety comes from Him, so that it is established in his mind that the source of security is Allaah.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Tranquility in Allaah and love of the source of his safety are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon security in Him rather than fear of any other.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to spread the greeting of peace (“al-Salaamu 3alaykum”) and to supplicate for safety, so that his tongue is nurtured upon spreading the peace (salaam) that is one of the names of Allaah.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is habituated to spread the greeting of peace among his household and to restrain his harm from people so that they are safe from him, so that he becomes [an example of] “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe,” and his limbs act in accordance with the veneration of al-Salaam.
The Name of Allaah: al-Mu’min (the Bestower of Security)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Mu’min” denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah that is truthful in its tidings and its promise, and that grants its servants security from being wronged and gives them safety; He is the One who confirms His messengers with signs, granting His allies security from the torment.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the two attributes of truthfulness in tidings and the granting of security.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails knowledge, power, justice, and mercy, and that His promise is true and is never broken: ﴿Indeed, Allaah does not fail in His promise﴾ [Aal 3Imraan 3:9].
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿the Perfection, the Bestower of Faith, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allaah above whatever they associate with Him﴾ [al-Hashr 59:23], and He said, concerning the truthfulness of His promise: ﴿And who is more truthful than Allaah in statement﴾ [al-Nisaa’ 4:122].
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: For Allaah is al-Mu’min, who is truthful in what He tells, who fulfills what He promises, and who grants His believing servants security from His torment; so whoever believes in Him, He grants him security, and whoever affirms His promise works for it. So when the servant knows that his Lord is al-Mu’min, he trusts in His promise and His threat.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that the promise of al-Mu’min is true and is never broken, so work for His Paradise trusting in His promise. Warning: that His threat is likewise true, so beware of His Fire, affirming His threat; for whoever denies His promise or His threat has denied al-Mu’min.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child is taught that Allaah is truthful and does not lie, and that everything He has told is true, so that the absolute affirmation of the tidings of Allaah is established in his mind.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Trust in the promise of Allaah and security in His protection are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon tranquility and truthfulness.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is habituated to truthfulness in his speech because his Lord is al-Mu’min, the Truthful, so that his tongue grows up truthful.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained to fulfill his promise and to discharge trusts (for trustworthiness (amaanah) is part of faith (iemaan)), so that his limbs act in accordance with the veneration of al-Mu’min.
The Name of Allaah: al-Wahhaab (the Ever-Giving)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Wahhaab” is of the form “fa33aal,” which denotes intensity, and so it denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah who is abundant in gifts and bestowals, who gives without recompense, without motive, and without being asked—a giving that is vast and unceasing.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of repeated, vast giving.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails absolute self-sufficiency, generosity, power, and mercy, and that whatever is in the hands of the creation is from His giving.
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾ [Aal 3Imraan 3:8], and He said: ﴿Or do they have the depositories of the mercy of your Lord, the Exalted in Might, the Bestower?﴾ [Saad 38:9].
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: For Allaah bestows children, provisions, knowledge, faith, and well-being without any counter-payment; His treasuries are full and never depleted, He gives to whoever asks Him and to whoever does not ask Him. So whoever knows that all he possesses is a gift from al-Wahhaab gives thanks to Him and does not attribute the bounty to himself, and asks of Him that which the creation is powerless to grant.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that the treasuries of al-Wahhaab are never depleted, so ask of Him your every need, small and great, for no giving can overwhelm Him. Warning: that whoever attributes His blessings to himself or to another, or asks the gift from someone other than Him in that which none but Allaah is able to grant, has been ignorant of al-Wahhaab.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child is taught that everything he is given is a gift from Allaah al-Wahhaab, so that it is established in his mind that the true Giver is Allaah, and that whatever people possess is from the giving of Allaah.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Love of al-Wahhaab, aspiration to His giving, and gratitude for His gifts are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon hope and thankfulness.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to ask of Allaah and to supplicate Him for his needs, and to praise Him for His bestowals, so that his tongue grows up asking of and giving thanks to al-Wahhaab.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained in giving and bestowing upon his brothers in emulation of al-Wahhaab, and in not being miserly with what Allaah has given him, so that his limbs act in accordance with love of al-Wahhaab.
The Name of Allaah: al-Barr (the Most Kind and Beneficent)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Barr” denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah, abundant in kindness, benevolence, and gentleness toward His servants, truthful in what He promises, whose kindness and benevolence encompass all His creation.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of vast kindness and benevolence.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails mercy, generosity, forbearance, and self-sufficiency, and that every good that reaches the servant is from His kindness.
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, we used to supplicate Him before. Indeed, it is He who is the Beneficent, the Merciful﴾ [al-Toer 52:28].
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: For Allaah’s kindness toward His servants is above every kindness; He shows benevolence to them while they do evil, He conceals [their faults] while they disobey, and He bestows His favor upon them before they ask Him. So whoever knows the kindness of his Lord feels ashamed to meet it with ingratitude, and treats his parents and Allaah’s creation with kindness in gratitude for the kindness of his Creator.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that al-Barr multiplies [the reward] for whoever does good, in benevolence, and loves those who do good, so do good and good will be done to you. Warning: that whoever meets the kindness of Allaah with evildoing and ingratitude has denied a tremendous favor.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child is taught that Allaah is abundant in benevolence toward him, and that every good he attains is from Allaah, so that the attribution of all bounty to Allaah is established in his mind.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Love of al-Barr, the Benevolent, and gratitude for His benevolence are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon gratitude and benevolence.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to praise and extol Allaah, and is habituated to treating his parents with kindness through good speech, so that his tongue is nurtured upon kindness (birr).
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained in benevolence toward his parents and his brothers in emulation of the kindness of Allaah, so that his limbs act in accordance with love of al-Barr.
The Name of Allaah: al-Wadoed (the Most Loving)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Wadoed” denotes, by full correspondence, two meanings: that He is the One who loves His allies and is affectionate toward them, and the One who is loved and cherished in the hearts of His allies; He loves the believers, and they love Him.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of love reaching His allies.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails mercy, generosity, and benevolence, and that His love entails His good pleasure, His nearness, and His giving to whomever He loves.
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Affectionate﴾ [al-Buroedj 85:14], and He said upon the tongue of Shu3ayb: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Affectionate﴾ [Hoed 11:90].
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: For Allaah loves those who repent often, those who purify themselves, those who do good, the patient, and the God-fearing, and He places for them affection in the hearts of people; and Allaah’s love for His servant is greater than the servant’s love for himself. So whoever knows that his Lord is al-Wadoed strives to attain His love through obeying Him.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that whomever Allaah loves, He casts love of him into the hearts and honors him in both abodes, so seek His love through obeying Him. Warning: that whoever disobeys Him and hates what He loves is deprived of His love, and Allaah despises him.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child is taught that Allaah loves him when he obeys Him, and that the love of Allaah is the greatest thing he can seek, so that the linking of love to obedience is established in his mind.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Love of Allaah and love of being loved by Allaah are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon love, not fear alone.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to say “I love Allaah” and to mention what Allaah loves, so that his tongue grows up filled with love of al-Wadoed.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained to do what Allaah loves (such as truthfulness and benevolence) so as to attain His love, so that his limbs act in accordance with love of al-Wadoed.
The Name of Allaah: al-Ra’oef (the Most Compassionate)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Ra’oef” denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah described with the perfection of compassion (ra’fah), which is the tenderest and most intense of mercy; He is merciful to His servants with a compassion that surpasses [ordinary] mercy in its tenderness.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of consummate compassion.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails mercy, forbearance, and gentleness, and that His compassion requires His lightening [of burdens] upon His servants and His gentleness with them.
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allaah is, to the people, Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143], and He said: ﴿And Allaah is Kind to [His] servants﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:207].
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: Among [the signs of] His compassion is that He has lightened the [religious] obligations and burdens no soul beyond its capacity, that He has legislated concessions (rukhas) in the event of hardship, and that He is gentle with His servants in His command and His prohibition; His compassion for the servant is greater than the compassion of a mother for her child. So whoever knows the compassion of his Lord is gentle with Allaah’s creation out of mercy toward them.
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that the compassion of Allaah lightens [your burden] for you and eases your affair, so seek it through a good opinion [of Allaah] and obedience. Warning: that whoever’s heart grows hard, so that he shows no mercy to the servants of Allaah, contravenes the compassion of his Lord.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child is taught that Allaah is gentle and more merciful to him than his own mother, so that the conception of the gentle God, not the harsh one, is established in his mind.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): Tranquility, gentleness, and love of al-Ra’oef are planted within him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon gentleness and mercy.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is habituated to the gentle, soft word with people, so that his tongue grows up gentle.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained in gentleness toward the young, the animal, and the servant, so that his limbs act in accordance with love of al-Ra’oef.
The Name of Allaah: al-Ghaffaar (the Perpetual Forgiver)
The meaning and its three modes of signification:
Signification by full correspondence (mutaabaqah): “al-Ghaffaar” is of the form “fa33aal,” [denoting] intensity, and it denotes, by full correspondence, the Essence of Allaah who is abundant in forgiveness, who conceals sins and remits them time after time for whoever seeks forgiveness and repents.
Signification by inclusion (tadammun): It includes the affirmation of the Essence and the attribute of repeated, vast forgiveness.
Signification by entailment (iltizaam): It entails forbearance, mercy, generosity, and power, and that the door of forgiveness is never closed.
The evidences from the Book and the Sunnah: Allaah the Exalted said: ﴿And said, “Ask forgiveness of your Lord. Indeed, He is ever a Perpetual Forgiver”﴾ [Noeh 71:10], and He said: ﴿But indeed, I am the Perpetual Forgiver of whoever repents and believes and does righteousness and then continues in guidance﴾ [Taahaa 20:82]. And in the sacred hadith (hadieth qudsie): “O My servants, you sin by night and by day, and I forgive all sins, so seek My forgiveness and I will forgive you” (Narrated by Muslim, no. 2577).
The scholarly and homiletic exposition: However often the servant’s sin recurs, the forgiveness of al-Ghaffaar is vaster; He conceals, remits, and forgives time after time for whoever turns back to Him. So let not the abundance of sin drive the servant to despair, nor let the vastness of forgiveness drive him to persistence [in sin].
Encouragement and warning (targhieb and tarhieb): Encouragement: that al-Ghaffaar forgives all sins for whoever seeks forgiveness, so hasten to seek forgiveness and do not despair. Warning: that forgiveness is for whoever repents, not for whoever persists, so do not be deluded and thereby procrastinate repentance until death takes you by surprise.
The pedagogical application across the four paths within this age group:
Through purging (tasfiyah): The child—now that he has begun to err—is taught that Allaah forgives and conceals [the faults of] whoever seeks forgiveness, so that it is established in his mind that a mistake is remedied by seeking forgiveness, not by despair.
Through purification of the soul (tazkiyah): The emotion of hope after a mistake and the hastening to seek forgiveness are planted within him, so that his soul is nurtured between fear and hope.
Through the cultivation of the tongue: He is taught to say “Astaghfiru Allaah (I seek Allaah’s forgiveness)” when he errs, so that his tongue is nurtured upon seeking forgiveness.
Through the cultivation of the limbs: He is trained—when he errs—to seek forgiveness and to repair his mistake, so that his limbs act in accordance with the hope [placed] in al-Ghaffaar.
The detailed innate characteristics specific to this developmental stage, and how to direct them pedagogically toward the veneration of Allaah and the governance and direction of the deeds of the hearts
1. The dawning of faith-consciousness: He poses questions about the purpose of life.
First: Addressing it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that the purpose of life is the worship of Allaah and love of Him. He links every question to this purpose in simple words that the child can take in.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in the child’s heart [the truth] that his greatest happiness lies in knowing Allaah. He shows joy before him at the mention of Paradise and the meeting with Allaah.
Third: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the tongue
He teaches the child to say “I was created to worship Allaah.” He asks him to repeat it daily at a fixed time.
Fourth: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the limbs
The educator takes the child by the hand so that he prays with him, even if only a short prostration. He makes praying with him a tangible daily habit.
Directing it through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator invests the child’s questions about [life’s] purpose to establish that he was created for the worship of Allaah, so that his soul is led to the knowledge of its true purpose.
Through leading the emotions: The educator links the child’s reflection upon [life’s] purpose to the love and veneration of Allaah, so that his emotion is nurtured upon reverence.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator habituates the child to seeking the truth in his purpose for the sake of Allaah, thereby planting sincerity of orientation.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the purpose that Allaah loves—namely His worship—and makes clear the falsehood of whoever lives for other than it, so that the child grows up upon loving and hating for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator answers the child’s existential questions with patience and gradualness, and does not rebuke him for asking.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator answers the child’s existential questions with gentleness and wisdom, counseling him by his own conduct to direct his curiosity toward knowing his Creator, and not rebuking him.
Through the governance of time: The educator seizes the moments of the child’s existential questioning to answer him with what suits his understanding, thereby investing his eagerness at its [proper] time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator fortifies the child against specious doubts (shubuhaat) that would divert him from his purpose, cast by Satan and the people of falsehood.
2. The capacity for partial abstract thought: The child begins to conceive of unseen realities (such as Paradise and the Fire), yet they remain tied to sensory images.
First: Addressing it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator describes Paradise and the Fire with sensory images that the child can take in (rivers, fruit, fire). He repeats them in the daily stories.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart love of Paradise and a tender fear of the Fire. He shows joy before him when the child wishes for Paradise.
Third: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the tongue
He asks him to say “O Allaah, admit me into Paradise and protect me from the Fire.” He repeats it with him daily, with joy.
Fourth: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the limbs
He supplicates with him and raises his hands so that he grows accustomed to the act of supplication. He makes this [a practice] after every prayer.
Directing it through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator invests the child’s conception of the unseen to firmly root faith in Paradise and the Fire, so that his soul is led, through hope and fear, to Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator plants in the child hope for Paradise and fear of the Fire in balance, so that his emotion is nurtured upon faith, not obsessive misgiving (waswaas).
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator habituates the child to work for Paradise seeking the Face of Allaah, thereby planting sincerity.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child what leads to Paradise and makes hateful to him what leads to the Fire, so that he grows up upon loving and hating for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator firmly roots faith in the unseen with patience and a gradualness suited to the child’s understanding.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator firmly roots faith in the unseen through example and gentleness, counseling him by his own conduct to affirm the tidings of Allaah and to submit to what is hidden from him.
Through the governance of time: The educator firmly roots faith in the unseen over gradual intervals suited to his understanding, so that his certainty grows through constancy, not through a single burst.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator fortifies the child’s faith in the unseen against the doubt-casting of Satan and the people of atheism.
3. A deeper grasp of the concept of lordship (ruboebiyyah): He realizes that Allaah is not seen and that He knows the unseen.
First: Addressing it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah is not seen but sees everything and knows the unseen. He gives simple examples that the child understands (the air, sound).
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart a sense of intimacy [in the knowledge] that Allaah is with him even if he does not see Him. He shows joy before him at the mention of the companionship (ma3iyyah) of Allaah.
Third: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the tongue
He teaches him to say “Allaah sees me, Allaah hears me, Allaah knows what is in my heart.” He repeats it with him daily.
Fourth: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the limbs
He reminds him, when he is alone, that Allaah sees him, so that he abandons wrongdoing even in solitude. He trains him through small situations.
Directing it through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator firmly roots in the child [the truth] that Allaah sees him and knows his secret, so that his soul is led, through mindfulness of Him (muraaqabah), to obedience.
Through leading the emotions: The educator plants in the child awe of Allaah, who knows the unseen, and love of Him, so that his emotion is nurtured upon reverence.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator habituates the child to mindfulness of Allaah in private and in public, thereby planting the foundation of sincerity.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child Allaah, the All-Knowing, and instills fear of Him in balance, so that he grows up upon love of Him and awe of Him.
Through patience (sabr): The educator firmly roots the meanings of lordship in the child with patience and facilitated repetition.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child the meanings of lordship in a facilitated manner and through example, counseling him by his own conduct to know his Lord, the Creator, the Provider.
Through the governance of time: The educator repeats the teaching of lordship at regular, facilitated intervals, so that it takes firm root in his heart through repetition.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator fortifies the child’s conception of his Lord against anthropomorphism (tashbieh) or divestment of the divine attributes (ta3tiel) cast by Satan and the purveyors of falsehood.
4. The increasing capacity for concentration: Following an activity or a story for a longer duration.
First: Addressing it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator invests the child’s concentration in teaching him a short verse or a remembrance (dhikr). He explains its meaning in words he understands.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart love of the Qur’an. He shows joy before him when the child memorizes a verse and praises him for it.
Third: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the tongue
He has him memorize a short verse each week. He asks him to recite it back with joy at a fixed time.
Fourth: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the limbs
He has him sit with him during recitation for a short, increasing duration. He makes it a daily routine together with the prayer.
Directing it through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator employs the child’s concentration in the memorization of the Qur’an and remembrance, thereby establishing a capacity by which the soul is led to goodness.
Through leading the emotions: The educator links the child’s concentration on goodness to joy and love, so that his emotion becomes bound to the atmosphere of obedience.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator habituates the child to directing his concentration to Allaah, thereby planting sincerity in his deeds.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator directs the child’s concentration toward what Allaah loves and turns it away from what He hates, so that the child grows familiar with goodness.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child to prolong his concentration on goodness with patience and gradualness.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to prolong his concentration on goodness through example, counseling him by his own conduct to complete what he has begun and not to become scattered.
Through the governance of time: The educator trains the child through short, graduated periods of concentration, extending them little by little until he masters his time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator fills the child’s concentration with what is beneficial, leaving no room in his mind for idle diversion that Satan might exploit.
5. The capacity to carry out multi-stage instructions.
First: Addressing it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator teaches the child that every step in the instructions is an opportunity for the remembrance of Allaah. He links it to the intention of pleasing Allaah.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart love of consecutive obedience. He shows joy before him when he completes it in full.
Third: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the tongue
He asks him to repeat the instructions before carrying them out. He repeats them with him so that he keeps them in mind.
Fourth: Addressing it through formation (tarbiyah) — the cultivation of the limbs
He assigns him tasks of three sequential steps (ablution, prayer, supplication). He praises him upon their completion, with joy.
Directing it through the branches of veneration:
Through leading the soul and seeking knowledge: The educator employs the child’s capacity in the steps of obedience, such as the stages of ablution, thereby establishing a submissiveness by which the soul is led to the command of Allaah.
Through leading the emotions: The educator links the child’s compliance to joy and love, so that the emotion of his obedience becomes bound to an intimacy with goodness.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator habituates the child to complying with the command of goodness for the sake of Allaah, not merely to please the educator himself.
Through love, fear, and loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child compliance with what Allaah loves and keeps him away from obeying whoever commands evil, so that he grows up upon loving and hating for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child to complete multi-stage tasks with patience and perseverance.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to complete his tasks through example, counseling him by his own conduct toward perseverance and mastery of what is in his hands.
Through the governance of time: The educator divides the task into stages across consecutive intervals, thereby habituating the child to accomplishing his work at its [proper] time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator habituates the child to complying with goodness, so that he does not grow up quick to obey the caller to evil.
6. Organized group play: Adhering to roles and the rules of the game.
First: Addressing it through purging (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that adhering to the rules and roles is part of the good character that Allaah loves. He links it to pleasing Allaah.
Second: Addressing it through purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of adhering to order for the sake of Allaah. He rejoices before him when he keeps to his turn without causing disruption.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “I keep to my turn for the sake of Allaah” during games. He repeats it with him daily in every play session.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He trains him to keep to his turn in small group games. He makes that into a tangible habit.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator teaches the child to abide by the rules of play, thereby establishing a discipline by which the self is led to observe the limits of Allaah.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator teaches the child to control his feelings during group play, and instills in him gentleness and fairness.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to playing well with his companions for the sake of Allaah and not merely for the sake of winning, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the justice and faithfulness towards his companions that Allaah loves, and keeps him away from cheating, so that he grows up upon love for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience and in keeping to his turn and the rules during play.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to keep to his turn and the rules by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to restrain himself and to observe the right of others.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator accustoms the child to abiding by the time of his turn and his round, thereby training him in the disciplining of time during play.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that cheating and injustice in play are from the adornment of Satan, and so keeps him away from it.
7. Love of competition: the desire to win and to assert oneself.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that the best of competition lies in good deeds and in obedience to Allaah. He invests his enthusiasm for that.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of vying in good deeds. He praises him when he outstrips others in a good deed.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “I hasten to do good” in every competition. He repeats it with him daily.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He provides him with a competition in memorizing a verse or a remembrance (dhikr). He praises him for doing good, not merely for winning.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator directs the child’s love of competition towards racing in good deeds, thereby establishing a resolve by which the self is led to obedience.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator regulates the child’s desire to win so that it does not turn into envy, and instills in him joy at another’s winning through good.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to competing for the sake of Allaah and His pleasure, not for boasting and self-assertion, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child competition in the good that Allaah loves, and keeps him away from blameworthy boasting, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience and contentment when losing, and accustoms him to not despairing.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child contentment when losing by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct not to despair and to hold a good opinion of Allaah.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator occupies the child with a new attempt at its proper time, thereby accustoming him to overcoming loss through action rather than through regret.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that the love of dominance may be dragged by Satan towards arrogance and envy, and so directs him towards praiseworthy competition.
8. The development of creative imagination: inventing stories and complex games.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
He explains to the child that imagination is a blessing meant to serve good. He directs him to compose stories about the righteous.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of creating what Allaah loves. He rejoices before him at stories he weaves about good.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to weave short stories about a child who loves Allaah. He listens to them from him and praises them.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He plays roles with him in which he acts out the Companions or the people of good. He repeats them alongside his usual games.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator directs the child’s creative imagination towards inventing what benefits in good, thereby establishing an ability by which the self is led to what Allaah loves.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator instills in the child’s creativity the love of good and the veneration of the Creator, so that his emotion is formed upon what is wholesome.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to employing his creativity for the sake of Allaah and not for showing off, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child inventing within the good that Allaah loves, and keeps him away from imagining evil, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator encourages the child’s creativity with patience and develops it gradually.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator encourages the child’s creativity by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to direct his talent towards what benefits and pleases Allaah.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator provides the child with regular times for creativity, thereby developing his talent in a fruitful rather than a wasted time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator safeguards the child’s imagination from being dragged by Satan towards imagining falsehood and the forbidden.
9. A growing sense of justice: objecting upon seeing injustice.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah commands justice and detests injustice. He invests his sense of justice in teaching him that.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of aiding the wronged for the sake of Allaah. He rejoices before him when he comes to the aid of the weak.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “No injustice; Allaah is just” in every situation. He repeats it with him gently.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He trains him to give his siblings their rights without diminution. He makes that a daily habit.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator instills in the child that justice is from Allaah and is His command, thereby establishing a concept by which the self is led to fairness.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator regulates the child’s anger upon seeing injustice, and transforms it into a controlled rejection rather than an emotional outburst.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to justice for the sake of Allaah, thereby instilling sincerity in his fairness.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the justice that Allaah loves, and makes injustice hateful to him, so that he grows up upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience and contentment with the decree of Allaah should an injustice befall him, together with rejecting it as is his right.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child patience in the face of injustice together with rejecting it as is his right, by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to be content with the decree and to seek his right with good manners.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator listens to the child for a sufficient time when he complains and then gives him his due, thereby accustoming him to patience until his right is secured.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that Satan loves injustice, and so endears justice to him and keeps him away from injustice.
10. The beginning of a relative grasp of time (today, tomorrow, yesterday).
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator invests the child’s understanding of time in reminding him of the times of prayer. He links each daily time period with a prayer or a remembrance (dhikr).
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart that every moment of time is a blessing that ought to be given thanks for. He rejoices before him when he says “Praise be to Allaah” in the morning and the evening.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to recite the morning and evening remembrances (adhkaar). He makes them a fixed daily routine.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He takes him to the prayer at its proper time. He keeps close to him in it so that he grasps the five prayer times in a practical way.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator links the child’s grasp of time to the times of worship, thereby establishing that time is a blessing by which the self is led to the obedience of Allaah.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator instills in the child the love of the times of good and the anticipation of them, so that his emotion becomes bound to the atmosphere of obedience.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to seizing his time for the sake of Allaah, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the seizing of time in what Allaah loves, and keeps him away from wasting it in what He detests, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience in awaiting good and not being hasty for it.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child to await good by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct not to be hasty and to trust in the planning of Allaah.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator accustoms the child to waiting a while for what he wants, thereby training him in deliberateness and in restraining his desire at its proper time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that wasting time in idle amusement is from the adornment of Satan, and so endears to him the seizing of it.
11. Attachment to specific friends.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that righteous companionship helps him in the worship of Allaah. He joyfully chooses righteous friends for him.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of friends for the sake of Allaah. He rejoices before him when he mentions a righteous friend.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “I love you for the sake of Allaah” to his righteous friend. He repeats it with him upon meeting.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He involves him in visiting righteous friends or playing with them in his presence. He multiplies such occasions.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator directs the child’s choice of friends towards the people of good, thereby establishing a companionship by which the self is led to what Allaah loves.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator regulates the child’s attachment to his friends so that it does not overwhelm the love of Allaah.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to befriending for the sake of Allaah, thereby instilling sincerity in his companionship.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the companionship of the people of good and loving them for the sake of Allaah, and keeps him away from bad company, so that he grows up upon loyalty and disavowal.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience and excellence in companionship and the bearing of a friend’s faults.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child excellence in companionship by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to bear his friend’s faults and to advise him gently.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator sets aside times of righteous companionship for the child, thereby developing his intimacy with the good in an organized time.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator safeguards the child from evil companions who are among the soldiers of Satan, thereby establishing the companionship of good.
12. The growing ability to control some emotions.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
He explains to the child that controlling the emotions is a patience that Allaah loves. He invests his emerging ability in that.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart an intimacy with patience for the sake of Allaah. He rejoices before him when he controls his anger or his sorrow.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He instructs him to say “Praise be to Allaah in every state” when agitated. He repeats it with him gently.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He teaches him to change his posture when angry (sitting down, performing ablution). He makes it a tangible habit.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator develops the child’s ability to control his emotions, thereby establishing the leadership of the self by which it is led to forbearance and obedience.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator teaches the child to direct his feelings rather than to suppress them: anger in its proper place, and joy in obedience.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to controlling his emotions out of consciousness of Allaah, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the feelings that Allaah loves, such as forbearance and mercy, and makes the blameworthy ones hateful to him, so that he grows up upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience in controlling his emotions in times of hardship.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to control his emotions in times of hardship by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to be forbearing and to say the words of return (istirdjaa3).
Through the disciplining of time: The educator gives the child time to calm down in his moment of intensity, thereby accustoming him to controlling his agitation in the very moment.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that unbridled emotions are a gateway for Satan, and so accustoms him to controlling them through seeking refuge in Allaah and through stillness.
13. Being strongly affected by the praise or blame of adults.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that the praise of Allaah is greater than the praise of people. He links every praise to the joy of Allaah.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the seeking of Allaah’s pleasure first. He rejoices before him when he takes comfort in the praise of Allaah rather than that of people.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “Praise be to Allaah; Allaah loves this” upon hearing praise. He repeats it with him.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
The educator praises the child by linking it to the pleasure of Allaah rather than to his achievement. He makes that his constant approach.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator directs the child’s susceptibility to praise and blame towards the pleasure of Allaah, thereby establishing that the standard is the pleasure of Allaah, by which the self is led.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator regulates the child’s joy at praise and his grief at blame, teaching him balance and consciousness of Allaah.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to acting for the pleasure of Allaah, not for the praise of people nor out of fear of their blame, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator links his praise and his blame to what Allaah loves and detests, so that the child grows up upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience in the face of people’s blame if he is in the right, and not to be deluded by their praise.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child patience in the face of blame if he is in the right, by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct neither to be deluded by praise nor to collapse at blame.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator trains the child not to occupy his time with people’s reactions, so that he directs his concern to his own work rather than to their talk.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator is wary of accustoming the child to acting for praise, thereby opening the door of ostentation (riyaa’) which Satan exploits.
14. The beginning of comparing oneself with others.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
He explains to the child that comparison ought to be in good rather than in worldly matters. He redirects his inclination towards vying in good deeds.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart contentment with what Allaah has given him. He rejoices before him when he gives thanks for His blessings.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “O Allaah, bless it” upon seeing a blessing in another. He instructs him in it instead of envy.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He trains him not to grieve over what others possess. He makes his conduct one of contentment with what Allaah has provided him.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator directs the child’s comparison of himself towards racing in good, thereby establishing a resolve by which the self is led to obedience.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator regulates the child’s comparison so that it bequeaths neither envy nor self-conceit, and instills in him contentment.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to looking to his own deed for the sake of Allaah rather than to comparison with people, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the emulation of the people of good, and keeps him away from envying them, so that he grows up upon love for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience and contentment with what Allaah has apportioned, and not to look with envy towards what others have.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child contentment with what Allaah has apportioned by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct not to look with envy towards what others have.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator occupies the child with giving thanks for what he has, at its proper time, thereby turning him away from a comparison that wastes his time and his heart.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that envy and self-conceit are from Satan, and so keeps him away from blameworthy comparison.
15. A growing love of experimentation and discovery: the simple sciences and nature.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator invests the child’s passion for knowledge in linking it to the Creator of the universe. He explains to him the signs of Allaah in His creation at every experiment.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the veneration of Allaah upon seeing the marvel of creation. He rejoices before him when he reflects upon it.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “Glory be to Allaah” at every discovery. He repeats it with him out in nature.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He takes him on short outings in nature. He reminds him during them of the making of Allaah.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator links the child’s scientific experiments to the greatness of the Creator, thereby establishing that knowledge is that by which one is led to the veneration of Allaah.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator links the child’s wonder at what he discovers to the veneration of its Maker, so that his emotion is formed upon reverence.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to seeking knowledge for the sake of knowing Allaah and being of benefit, not for boasting, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator directs the child’s discovery towards the beneficial knowledge that Allaah loves, and turns him away from what harms, so that he grows familiar with good.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience and perseverance in learning and experimentation.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child in perseverance in learning by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to be patient with the hardship of knowledge.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator sets aside regular, gradual times for learning, thereby accustoming the child to perseverance at its proper time without exhaustion.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator fortifies the child’s knowledge against being employed in what harms or turns away from Allaah through the adornment of Satan.
16. Awareness of social rules: “this is forbidden,” “this is obligatory.”
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
He explains to the child that the lawful and the forbidden are greater than people’s “not allowed.” He invests his understanding of rules in teaching him the rulings of Allaah.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of the lawful and the hatred of the forbidden. He rejoices before him when he leaves a small forbidden thing.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He instructs him to say “Allaah dislikes this” concerning minor forbidden things. He repeats it with him tenderly.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He trains him to abandon a simple religiously forbidden matter (refraining from eating something unlawful). He praises him for the abandonment through the joy of Allaah.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator links the child’s awareness of the forbidden and the obligatory to the limits of Allaah, thereby establishing that the reference is the law of Allaah, by which the self is led.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator instills in the child the love of adhering to good and the aversion to transgression, so that his emotion is formed upon what is wholesome.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to adhering to good for the sake of Allaah and not merely out of social custom, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator teaches the child that the greatest of what is forbidden is what Allaah has forbidden, and the most binding of the obligatory is what He has made obligatory, so that he grows up upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator trains the child in patience in observing the limits even if others transgress them.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator trains the child to observe the limits even if others transgress them, by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to remain steadfast upon the truth.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator fixes the child’s limits firmly at all his times, so that his adherence to them becomes deeply rooted through constancy.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that transgressing the limits of Allaah gladdens Satan, and so endears to him the observance of them.
17. A clearer grasp of the difference between truthfulness and lying.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator explains to the child that Allaah loves truthfulness and dislikes lying. He invests his ability to distinguish.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of truthfulness. He rejoices before him when he tells the truth even if it exposes himself.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He instructs him to say “Truthfulness is salvation; Allaah loves the truthful.” He repeats it with him daily.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He rewards him for truthfulness with the pleasure of Allaah before him. He makes that his constant approach.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator instills in the child the love of truthfulness and the ugliness of lying, thereby establishing a character trait by which the self is led to what Allaah loves.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator instills in the child the ease of the truthful and the anxiety of the liar, so that his emotion is formed upon the love of truthfulness.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to truthfulness with Allaah and with people for the sake of Allaah, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the truthfulness that Allaah loves, and makes lying hateful to him, so that he grows up upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience in speaking the truth even if it is hard, and not to lie in order to escape.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child truthfulness even if it is hard, by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to be truthful and not to lie in order to escape.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator seizes the child’s situations to accustom him to truthfulness at their very moment, thereby investing the moment in the entrenchment of truthfulness.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that lying leads to wickedness and that Satan loves it, and so keeps him away from it.
18. Love of stories that carry a lesson or wisdom.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator selects for the child Qur’anic and prophetic stories that he can understand. He explains their lesson in simplified words.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of the prophets and the Companions. He rejoices before him when he hears their stories.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to tell the story to his siblings. He praises him for it joyfully.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He puts into practice with him a deed from the story in real life. He makes that a practical entrenchment.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator uses stories that carry a lesson to entrench good, thereby establishing a reference by which the self is led to what Allaah loves.
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator instills through the stories the love of good and its people and the hatred of evil, so that the child’s emotion is formed upon what is wholesome.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to taking the lesson and acting upon it for the sake of Allaah, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator relates the stories of those whom Allaah has loved and warns against the people of evil, so that he grows up upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator relates the stories of the patient in order to endear patience to the child, and repeats them until they become deeply rooted.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator relates the stories of the patient by way of example, counseling the child through their state to emulate them and to be patient upon good.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator sets aside a regular time for the stories of the righteous, so that the love of emulating them becomes deeply rooted through constancy.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator relates stories that make clear the plotting of Satan and his enmity, thereby acquainting the child with his enemy and fortifying him.
19. Showing compassion towards animals or younger children.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
He explains to the child that mercy towards creation is a cause for the mercy of Allaah. He invests his compassion in teaching him that.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart mercy for the destitute and the weak. He rejoices before him when he shows mercy to a younger sibling.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “O Allaah, have mercy on us as we show mercy” in situations of mercy. He repeats it with him.
Fourthly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the limbs
He involves him in feeding a bird or watering a plant. He repeats these actions daily.
Governance through the branches of veneration (ta3dhiem):
Through the leadership of the self and the pursuit of knowledge: The educator instills in the child that Allaah loves mercy, thereby establishing a character trait by which the self is led to excellence (ihsaan).
Through the leadership of the emotions: The educator develops the child’s mercy and directs it, so that his emotion is formed upon gentleness towards the creation of Allaah.
Through sincerity (ikhlaas): The educator accustoms the child to mercy for the sake of Allaah and not to be seen as merciful, thereby instilling sincerity.
Through love, fear, loyalty and disavowal (al-walaa’ wa-l-baraa’): The educator endears to the child the mercy that Allaah loves, and makes cruelty hateful to him, so that he grows up upon love and hatred for the sake of Allaah.
Through patience (sabr): The educator teaches the child patience in showing excellence to the weak and caring for him.
Through sincere counsel (nasiehah): The educator teaches the child excellence towards the weak by way of example, counseling him through his own conduct to show mercy and to care for those below him.
Through the disciplining of time: The educator provides the child with occasions of excellence at their proper times, thereby accustoming him to caring for the weak at the appropriate moment.
Through knowing the enemies: The educator teaches the child that cruelty and harming are from the adornment of Satan, and so endears mercy to him.
20. Attempting to help with real tasks.
Firstly: Addressing it through purging and refinement (tasfiyah)
The educator invests the child’s desire to help by linking it to the joy of Allaah. He explains to him that serving one’s family is an act of worship.
Secondly: Addressing it through the purification of the soul (tazkiyah)
He plants in his heart the love of serving the family. He rejoices before him when he helps, with joy.
Thirdly: Addressing it through upbringing and formation (tarbiyah) — the training of the tongue
He asks him to say “I help you for the sake of Allaah, my mother/father.” He repeats it with him before the task.
